content:
There is a lot of excitement around AI-enabled modernisation, and with good reason. Analysis can be accelerated, code can be generated or transformed faster, testing can be improved, and large estates that once looked prohibitively expensive to tackle can begin to look much more manageable. But that creates a new problem: if the technology can move faster, how much change can the organisation actually absorb?
That question is rarely asked clearly enough at the beginning of a modernisation programme. We tend to model engineering capacity, delivery waves, migration throughput, environments and technical dependencies in some detail, but we do not always model with the same discipline the capacity of the organisation itself to consume the change being produced. That matters because transformation is not complete when the new capability exists. It is complete when the organisation has actually moved.
This follows directly from the problem I explored in Scaling AI Modernisation Means Scaling Decisions, Not Just Code: once we start treating modernisation as a flow rather than a code-generation problem, organisational capacity becomes another constraint in that flow.
AI changes expectations as well as delivery # There is another dynamic emerging around this. Clients increasingly expect AI-enabled programmes to be quicker, cheaper and better. That expectation is understandable because the wider narrative around AI strongly suggests that delivery should accelerate, cost should fall and quality should improve at the same time.
Sometimes that expectation is justified, but it can also create a significant expectation differential between what AI can accelerate technically and what the wider organisation can absorb operationally. A supplier may genuinely be able to analyse an application estate faster, generate transformations more quickly, automate more testing and reduce the effort needed for repetitive engineering work. None of that automatically makes business validation, regulatory approval, user adoption, operational readiness or organisational decision-making move at the same speed.
The danger is that the client hears “AI makes modernisation faster” and reasonably concludes that the whole programme should compress in proportion. That is where tension starts to appear, because the engineering portion of the work may shrink significantly while many of the non-engineering constraints remain largely unchanged. If those constraints are not made visible early, the programme can appear slower than expected even while the technology component is performing extremely well.
AI can therefore improve the capability of one part of the system while making the limits of the rest of the system much more obvious.
Transformation has an absorption limit # Most organisations have a finite ability to deal with concurrent change. People still have day jobs. Operational teams still need to run services. Managers still need to support teams. Front-line workers still need to learn new processes, subject-matter experts still need to validate decisions, and governance functions still need to review changes.
There is a point beyond which more change does not mean more progress. It simply creates more work in progress.
This is particularly important where modernisation affects how people work day to day. A platform change may look technical from the programme perspective while changing access patterns, controls, approvals, reporting, support routes or operational procedures for the people using it. Those impacts accumulate, and an organisation may be perfectly capable of absorbing one or two significant changes in a period but not ten.
The technical programme may have capacity for ten. The organisation may not. That difference becomes a constraint on the whole system.
The field-of-dreams problem # This is where some IT-led transformations start to become “build it and they will come” programmes. The new platform is built, the new process is available, the migration is technically possible, and the assumption is that adoption will naturally follow.
Sometimes it does. Often only part of the organisation moves.
That can leave the organisation in a worse position than before because the new platform now has to be operated, but the old platform cannot be retired. Some users follow the new process while others remain on the old one. Support teams have to deal with both, controls may exist in two places, reporting becomes fragmented, and the original risk or cost the programme was meant to remove still exists because the old estate has not actually disappeared.
The transformation has delivered change, but not completion. That is why one of the most useful measures of transformation is not simply whether the new capability has gone live, but whether the old capability can be turned off.
A transformation is not complete when the new capability exists. It is complete when the old way of working is no longer required.
That is a much harder standard, but a much more meaningful one.
Change capacity is not constant # Another mistake we make is assuming that organisational capacity is broadly stable over time. It is not.
Most organisations have predictable periods when their ability to absorb change drops significantly. Common examples include:
regulatory freezes that limit production change; financial year-end, when finance, operations and leadership teams are heavily constrained; peak trading periods where operational stability takes precedence; major audits, reporting cycles or annual planning windows; business-critical periods where certain changes are simply too disruptive. These are not exceptional events. They are part of the operating environment.
If we were modelling an engineering system, we would treat this as capacity variation. Yet transformation programmes often build plans that assume the organisation is equally available throughout the year and then describe the resulting delays as stakeholder issues.
A more useful model would make those constraints explicit.
flowchart LR A[Engineering Capacity] --> C[Transformation Throughput] B[Business Change Capacity] --> C D[Environment Capacity] --> C E[Decision / SME Capacity] --> C F[Year End / Regulatory Freeze / Peak Period] F -. reduces .-> B F -. reduces .-> D F -. reduces .-> EThe throughput of the transformation is constrained by the lowest available capacity across the system, not simply by the speed at which engineering work can be produced.
Shorter programmes make these constraints more important # This becomes particularly significant in an AI-enabled modernisation programme because one of the promises is that the programme itself becomes shorter. If AI allows us to analyse and transform an estate in months rather than years, then a six-week regulatory freeze or an unavailable business-validation team becomes proportionally much more significant.
A pause that represented a small percentage of a multi-year programme can become a major part of a compressed delivery window. That creates a practical challenge for suppliers as well: if the engineering team can continue working but the client cannot validate, approve or provide subject-matter expertise, what should the delivery organisation do during that period?
The traditional answer is often to keep producing:
continue analysing applications; continue generating code; continue preparing migrations; build a backlog ready for when the client becomes available again. But that can create exactly the WIP problem we should be trying to avoid. The supplier looks productive because work continues to be generated, but the programme accumulates a growing queue of unvalidated change. When the client becomes available again, they are no longer faced with one decision or one migration; they are faced with dozens.
That does not improve flow. It simply moves the bottleneck.
Keep the team valuable, not merely busy # This changes the supplier question from “How do we keep the team busy while the client is unavailable?” to “What work increases future throughput while the primary flow is constrained?”
A regulatory freeze may prevent deployment but not estate discovery. Business SMEs may be unavailable for validation while dependency information is improved. Production change may be restricted while automated testing, migration archetypes, code semantics, observability or environment readiness are strengthened.
The important distinction is between work that creates more inventory and work that improves the system’s ability to process future change. Generating another hundred unvalidated migrations may simply increase WIP, while improving test automation, dependency confidence or the semantic model of the estate may increase the speed at which those migrations can safely move once the constraint is removed.
That is particularly important in outsourced delivery, where commercial pressure can easily reward visible activity rather than genuine system improvement.
Change should be modelled like any other dependency # We already accept that technical systems have dependency chains. Application B may need to move before application C, a shared service may need to be upgraded before a downstream application can transition, or a test environment may need to be available before a release can proceed.
Organisations have dependency chains too. A team may need training before a process changes. A manager may need access to new reporting before an old control can be removed. A service desk may need new support capability before a platform goes live. A policy may need to change before behaviour can safely follow.
These are not just communications tasks. They are dependencies in the transformation flow.
Once we treat them that way, the programme becomes much easier to reason about. The question becomes: what has to be true before this change can safely move to the next state?
That is exactly the same reasoning we apply to technical modernisation.
Calendar constraints can become part of the model # There is an interesting AI implication here as well. If a modernisation system already understands dependencies, migration archetypes, environments and decision rights, there is no reason it cannot also understand organisational calendars and operating constraints.
It can know that:
a particular application group cannot deploy during a regulatory freeze; finance SMEs have sharply reduced availability around year-end; a critical operational function has a restricted change window; a particular environment is unavailable during another programme’s testing cycle. Those constraints can be treated as part of the migration route in exactly the same way as a technical dependency. That means the system can sequence work around the organisation rather than discovering those constraints after the work has already been prepared.
This is an important evolution of the idea of enterprise context. Enterprise context is not just technical context; it also includes how the organisation actually operates.
Faster delivery can expose slower adoption # There is a broader consequence here. AI may dramatically increase our capacity to produce change, but if organisational absorption capacity does not increase at the same rate, then the bottleneck simply moves.
We may end up with technically complete capabilities waiting for:
training; validation; policy changes; operational readiness; business adoption. That is effectively the same queueing problem as code waiting for a test environment. The difference is that the queue is now made up of people, decisions and operating processes.
This is why the client expectation of “faster, cheaper, better” needs to be handled carefully. The promise should not simply be that every part of the programme becomes faster because AI is present. The better promise is that AI allows us to compress the parts of the flow that can genuinely be accelerated, while giving us better visibility of the constraints that cannot.
That creates a more realistic and useful conversation about where time and cost can actually be removed.
The real measure is whether the old world disappears # The organisations that get this right will not simply become better at delivering change. They will become better at understanding how much change they can absorb, where that capacity sits, how it varies over time and how to sequence transformation around it.
That matters because building the future state is only half the job. The value appears when the organisation can leave the old state behind.
AI may significantly increase our capacity to produce change. That makes understanding the organisation’s capacity to consume change more important, not less.
summary:
There is a lot of excitement around AI-enabled modernisation, and with good reason. Analysis can be accelerated, code can be generated or transformed faster, testing can be improved, and large estates that once looked prohibitively expensive to tackle can begin to look much more manageable. That question is rarely asked clearly enough at the beginning of a modernisation programme. That matters because transformation is not complete when the new capability exists. It is complete when the organisation has actually moved.

title: John, Complected

content:
Read: Scripture Luke 1:5–25 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 91 NIV There are seasons in life when we wait much longer than we expected. We pray, hope and trust, and sometimes wonder whether anything is changing at all. Some answers come quickly, while others seem to take years. In those long seasons, it can be easy to wonder whether God has forgotten us.
The story of Zechariah and Elizabeth reminds us that waiting is not the same as being forgotten. They had lived faithfully for many years, prayed, served God and carried disappointment. By the time we meet them in Luke’s Gospel, they are both old, and the possibility of having a child seems to have passed.
And then God speaks.
Remember Zechariah and Elizabeth # Luke tells us that Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous before God and lived faithfully. Their disappointment did not mean they had been abandoned, and their age did not mean God was finished with them.
One day, while Zechariah was serving in the temple, an angel appeared to him and said:
Scripture Luke 1:13 NIV That sentence carries a great deal of hope: your prayer has been heard.
We are not told exactly how long Zechariah and Elizabeth had prayed for a child, but it had clearly been a long time. Perhaps there had been seasons when they prayed often and seasons when the prayer became quieter. Whatever those years looked like, God had not forgotten. His timing was different from theirs, but his silence had not meant absence.
Faithful in the Waiting # Waiting can sometimes feel like nothing is happening, but Scripture shows us again and again that God can be at work long before we can see the result.
Zechariah and Elizabeth could not see the whole story. They did not yet know that their son would become John the Baptist, that he would prepare the way for Jesus, or that their family would become part of something much larger than they had imagined. What looked like a late answer was actually part of a much bigger plan.
That does not mean every prayer is answered in exactly the way we expect. It does mean that God remains faithful even when we cannot yet see what he is doing.
Under His Wings # Psalm 91 gives us a picture of security and rest:
Scripture Psalm 91:4 NIV There is something gentle about that picture. To be under God’s wings is to be close to him, resting in his care rather than trying to understand every part of the future.
You do not need to have every answer today or know exactly how every prayer will be answered. You can rest in the truth that God sees you, knows you and has not forgotten you.
There Can Still Be Something New # Zechariah and Elizabeth had reached a point in life when they might reasonably have expected no major surprises, but God still had something new for them. Their story reminds us that later chapters are not empty chapters.
There can still be:
unexpected joy; prayers answered in surprising ways; new relationships to enjoy; new people to encourage; new things to learn; new ways to serve and bless others. God is not limited by the stage of life we are in. He is still able to lead, surprise, encourage and use us.
Rest While You Wait # Sometimes faith looks like moving forward boldly, as it did with Caleb, and sometimes faith looks like resting.
Zechariah and Elizabeth had already spent years being faithful. They did not have to force the next chapter into existence; God brought it in his time. There is freedom in that.
You can keep praying without carrying the whole weight of the answer. You can keep trusting without knowing exactly what comes next. You can keep living faithfully today while leaving tomorrow in God’s hands.
Remember # Zechariah and Elizabeth remind us that God does not measure our lives by speed. A long wait does not mean a forgotten prayer, and a later season does not mean an empty one.
Remember:
God has not forgotten you. He hears your prayers. He is faithful in the waiting. You are still under his care. There can still be new things ahead. God is not finished with you. Say this together # God has not forgotten me. I am under his care. He hears my prayers. He is faithful while I wait. There can still be new things ahead. God is not finished with me.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you see me and know me completely. Thank you for Zechariah and Elizabeth and for the reminder that you had not forgotten them, even after many years of waiting.
Help me to trust you when I cannot see what you are doing. Teach me to rest under your care and to leave the future in your hands.
Thank you that there can still be new things ahead, new ways to bless others and new reasons for joy. Keep me close to you, and help me to live faithfully today while trusting you with tomorrow.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

title: Remember Who You Are — Under His Wings

content:
Read: Scripture Joshua 14:6–14 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 23 NIV There is something powerful about looking back and seeing how faithfully God has led you.
There are seasons when the path has been clear and seasons when it has not. There are prayers that were answered quickly and others that took years. There are moments of joy, disappointment, waiting, change and unexpected blessing.
And through all of it, God has been faithful.
Psalm 23 begins with one of the simplest and strongest pictures in Scripture:
Scripture Psalm 23:1 NIV A shepherd does not only protect the sheep. He leads them. He brings them to good places. He restores them. He stays with them on the journey.
That means we are not only people who can look back and say, “God was faithful then.”
We can also say, “God is still leading me now.”
Remember Caleb # Caleb had waited a long time.
He had been one of the twelve spies sent into the land many years earlier. While most of the others saw only the size of the obstacles, Caleb trusted that God would be faithful to what he had promised.
Then came years of waiting.
By the time we meet Caleb again in Joshua 14, he is around eighty-five years old. He has lived through the wilderness years, seen a generation pass away and watched God fulfil his promises to Israel.
It would have been understandable for Caleb simply to look back and be thankful.
But that is not what he does.
He says:
Scripture Joshua 14:12 NIV There is no sense that Caleb thinks his useful years are behind him. He is grateful for what God has done, but he is still looking forward.
He still believes there is something ahead.
Still Looking Forward # Caleb’s confidence is not really about strength or personality. It is rooted in the faithfulness of God.
He can look back across decades and say, in effect, the God who kept me then will keep me now.
That is a powerful way to live.
You do not have to pretend that nothing has changed. Life does change. Energy changes. Responsibilities change. The shape of the journey changes.
But change does not mean the journey is over.
There can still be:
people to encourage; prayers to pray; wisdom to share; relationships to deepen; faith to pass on; new things to receive from God. Caleb teaches us that later life is not only about remembering what God has done. It can also be about asking, “Lord, what are you still leading me into?”
The Shepherd Still Leads # Psalm 23 is full of movement.
The Shepherd:
leads beside quiet waters; refreshes the soul; guides along right paths; walks with us through dark valleys; prepares a table; brings us into his goodness and love. This is not a picture of a God who brought us safely this far and then stepped away.
It is a picture of a God who keeps leading.
You may not know what every part of the road ahead looks like. Caleb did not know every detail either. But he knew enough to keep trusting the God who had been faithful all his life.
That is enough for today too.
There Is More Ahead # Sometimes we can become very good at talking about what God did in the past.
Those stories matter. They remind us of his faithfulness.
But they are not the whole story.
If you are still here, there is still a today to live with God.
There is still kindness to give, encouragement to speak, prayer to offer and love to share.
There are still people who need what God has placed in you.
There may even be new things you have not yet imagined.
God is not finished with you.
Caleb had history with God, but he also had expectation.
That is a beautiful combination: gratitude for what God has done and faith for what he will still do.
Remember # Caleb could look back over many years and see the faithfulness of God. That history did not make him passive. It made him confident.
Remember:
The Lord is your Shepherd. He has led you faithfully. He is leading you still. There is still purpose ahead. There is still something to give. God is not finished with you. Say this together # The Lord is my Shepherd. He has led me faithfully. He is leading me still. There is more ahead. God is not finished with me.
Prayer # Father, thank you for every way you have led me through the years. Thank you for the times I could see what you were doing and for the times when I simply had to trust you.
Thank you for Caleb and for the reminder that a long history with you can become a reason to keep looking forward.
Help me to recognise what you are still doing in my life. Show me where I can encourage, pray, bless and serve. Give me faith for what is ahead, and help me to keep following you one step at a time.
Thank you that you are my Shepherd, that you are with me now, and that you are still leading me.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

content:
There is a growing assumption in software modernisation that AI will allow us to industrialise the analysis and transformation of existing estates. Give a model a codebase, define the target architecture and increasingly it can analyse, refactor, generate tests and produce a substantial amount of the target implementation.
There is clearly value in that, but the idea becomes much harder when we move from an individual application to an enterprise estate. The problem is not simply that organisations use different technologies. There can be enormous variation between two applications built in the same language, by the same organisation and notionally against the same standards. Years of design decisions, local conventions, framework choices, technical debt, developer preferences and changing architectural standards leave each application carrying part of its own history.
That makes the idea of a single modernisation flow difficult. Even where the destination is common, the route to get there may not be.
The difficult part is the decision # Consider something that sounds relatively straightforward: an organisation wants to move its applications onto a common authentication authority.
At first glance, this looks like exactly the kind of repetitive change we should be able to automate. Identify the existing authentication implementation, replace it with the target mechanism, generate the necessary configuration and tests, and move on to the next application.
The reality is much more complicated. The estate may contain applications using different authentication patterns, different libraries and different generations of standards. Some applications may authenticate users directly, others may delegate authentication through another service, and still others may rely on authentication established somewhere upstream. There may be machine-to-machine identities, service accounts, token exchanges, legacy protocols and bespoke implementations accumulated over many years.
Even if the code transformation for each archetype can be automated, selecting the correct transformation requires context. Then there is another problem: sequence.
An application rarely exists alone. If one service changes its authentication mechanism while a dependent service still expects the previous identity or token model, a technically correct migration can still break the wider system.
The modernisation problem is therefore not just:
How do we change this application?
It is also:
What kind of application is this, what depends upon it, which migration path is appropriate, how confident are we in that classification, and when is it safe to make the change?
That is a very different problem from code generation.
Model the migration, not just the target # This is where I think some of the thinking we already apply to business value streams becomes useful in technology modernisation.
If this were a deployment or continuous-delivery problem, we would already be inclined to map the value stream. We would look at where work waits, where approvals happen, where environments constrain flow, where testing becomes a bottleneck and where hand-offs introduce delay or risk.
Modernisation should be treated the same way.
In fact, I would argue the need is greater because the system is often operating across a transitional architecture rather than a steady-state one. Existing applications, target platforms, temporary integration patterns, shared environments and different migration waves all coexist for a period of time. That creates constraints which are easy to overlook if the modernisation programme is viewed primarily as a code-transformation exercise.
Rather than defining a single prompt or transformation pipeline and applying it repeatedly, we can model the migration states and the decisions required to move between them.
For an authentication migration, for example, the organisation might identify a number of recurring archetypes across the estate. Each archetype can have known preconditions, transformation patterns, validation requirements and dependencies that must be satisfied before it is allowed to progress.
A conceptual modernisation flow might look like this:
flowchart LR A[Discover] --> B[Classify] B --> C[Dependency Analysis] C --> D[Select Migration Pattern] D --> E[Transform] E --> F[Validate] F --> G[Release] G --> H[Observe] X[(Enterprise Context)] X -.-> A X -.-> B X -.-> C X -.-> D X -.-> E X -.-> F X -.-> G X -.-> HThe important part is that each transition can have an explicit decision associated with it.
What evidence is required before an application can be classified? How confident must the system be before it is allowed to select a migration pattern? What dependencies have to be migrated first? Which tests demonstrate that the change has preserved the required behaviour? At what point does a human need to intervene?
Once those decisions are explicit, we can start asking a much more useful question about AI.
Not simply “Can AI perform the migration?”, but “What authority should we give each agent at each point in the migration?”
Faster code can still create slower flow # This is where I think a lot of modernisation thinking risks falling into the same trap that delivery teams have been trying to remove for years.
If we optimise only the transformation step, we may make one part of the system significantly faster while the rest of the flow remains constrained. The result is not necessarily faster delivery. It may simply be more work in progress.
A simplified current-state flow often looks something like this:
flowchart LR A[Applications Identified] --> B[AI / Engineering Analysis] B --> C[Code Changes Produced] C --> D[Human Review] D --> E[Test Environment] E --> F[Integration Testing] F --> G[Architecture / Security Approval] G --> H[Release] D -. WIP builds .-> D E -. Environment constraint .-> E F -. Dependency failures .-> F G -. Approval queue .-> GIf AI makes the analysis and code-production steps dramatically faster, but human review, test environments, integration testing and approvals remain fixed, then the system simply pushes more change into the constrained parts of the flow.
That is why the transitional constraints around testing and environments need to be front and centre rather than treated as downstream delivery concerns. They do not go away because AI can produce more code. If anything, they become more important because the rate at which change can be generated increases.
The modernisation problem is therefore not simply one of producing transformation capacity. It is one of managing flow across the entire migration system.
Autonomy should vary through the flow # Not every decision deserves the same level of autonomy.
An agent might have complete authority to inspect repositories, identify frameworks, build dependency information and compare an application against known migration archetypes. There may be little value in requiring human approval for every one of those activities.
The same agent might then recommend a migration route with an associated confidence level. For a well-understood pattern with strong evidence and comprehensive automated testing, the organisation may allow the transformation to proceed automatically. For an unusual implementation, low-confidence classification or particularly critical application, the decision may be escalated to an engineer or architect.
That creates a spectrum of agency rather than a binary choice between manual delivery and fully autonomous AI.
More importantly, the decision about autonomy is made deliberately. It becomes part of the architecture of the modernisation system rather than something implied by whichever AI tooling happens to be used.
A simple way of thinking about that is:
flowchart LR A[Known ArchetypeStrong Dependency DataHigh Test Coverage] --> B[High Confidence] B --> C[Greater Agent Autonomy] D[Unusual PatternWeak Dependency DataLimited Tests] --> E[Low Confidence] E --> F[Human Decision Required]The objective is not maximum autonomy. It is the highest level of autonomy that the available evidence can justify.
Transitional architecture is where the risk lives # Modernisation programmes rarely move cleanly from an old state to a new one. For months or years, organisations operate across both.
That means the migration system has to understand not just the target architecture, but the transitional architecture: which components have moved, which have not, which interfaces remain backward-compatible, which environments are shared, which tests are available and which temporary controls are currently keeping the whole thing together.
This matters particularly for authentication, because identity is rarely isolated to one application. A service may issue tokens consumed elsewhere, depend on another system for user context, or be part of a chain where different components move at different times. Changing one application correctly can still break the overall flow if the transition sequence is wrong.
For example:
flowchart LR A[Application AIssues Token] --> B[Application B] A --> C[Application C] C --> D[Application D] C --> E[Application E]All five applications may be individually suitable for transformation. That does not mean they can be migrated independently.
The migration sequence is constrained by the relationships between them.
The same applies more broadly across data, integration, networking, runtime platforms and deployment pipelines. That is why testing and environments have to be treated as part of the migration decision itself. If a test environment cannot accurately represent a transitional state, or if multiple applications must move together because of a dependency chain, that is part of the modernisation model.
The agentic system needs to reason about those constraints before transformation, not discover them after code has already been generated.
Enterprise context changes what an agent can know # This is where a semantic understanding of the wider estate becomes particularly important.
A coding agent operating against one repository can understand a surprising amount about that repository. What it cannot easily understand is everything that exists outside it: which other systems call the application, which business capabilities depend upon it, who owns it, what runtime constraints apply, which architectural decisions govern it, and what other migrations are already underway.
At enterprise scale, that context can be as important as the code itself.
A knowledge graph or equivalent semantic model can represent relationships between applications, APIs, identities, infrastructure, teams, business capabilities and architectural standards. The agent examining an authentication implementation no longer sees merely a library that needs replacing; it can understand where the application sits within a wider dependency chain.
This is where scaling the semantic knowledge of the estate becomes particularly powerful. The organisation is no longer relying on each agent to rediscover the estate one repository at a time. Instead, agents can reason against a shared enterprise context that captures both technical and organisational relationships.
The code is only part of the truth.
Agents need different responsibilities # This also suggests that a modernisation system should probably not be thought of as one enormously capable coding agent.
Different agents can operate against different parts of the problem. One may specialise in estate discovery and classification, another in dependency analysis, another in selecting transformation patterns, and another in generating or modifying code. Validation agents can examine tests, architecture conformance, security controls and behaviour, while orchestration coordinates the progression of an application through the migration flow.
The important thing is not the number of agents. It is that their responsibilities, evidence and decision rights are explicit.
That makes the system considerably easier to reason about than asking a general-purpose agent to inspect an application and “modernise it”.
It also gives us a much stronger basis for trust. If an agent selects migration pattern three, we should be able to understand why. Which characteristics of the application caused that classification? Which dependencies were considered? Which architectural rules were applied? What evidence gave the system sufficient confidence to proceed?
The interesting output of the system is therefore not simply transformed code.
It is a traceable chain of decisions that resulted in that code being transformed.
Scaling confidence alongside delivery # This becomes particularly important when organisations try to industrialise modernisation.
If we accelerate code generation without accelerating our ability to understand and validate the decisions surrounding it, we simply move the bottleneck. Engineers and architects become responsible for reviewing an increasingly large volume of AI-generated change, and eventually the human-in-the-loop becomes the constraint.
This is also where the discussion about dark factories becomes more useful.
There is an understandable attraction to the idea of a largely automated software delivery system where agents can analyse, change, test and deploy software with minimal human intervention. But autonomy should not be treated as the objective in itself.
The real objective is confidence sufficient to justify autonomy.
A dark factory is only valuable if the organisation understands why the system is allowed to proceed. That confidence cannot come from code-generation quality alone. It has to come from the surrounding evidence: known migration archetypes, validated dependency models, reliable tests, architecture policies, environment readiness, security controls and clear rules about where human judgement is still required.
In that sense, modelling the modernisation value stream is not separate from the dark-factory ambition. It is what makes it credible.
The more explicitly we can describe the migration states, decision rights, evidence and constraints, the more safely we can increase autonomy. A well-understood migration pattern with strong automated testing and no unresolved dependency risk might move almost entirely through an automated path. An unusual application with weak test coverage, undocumented dependencies or a shared legacy environment should not.
That is not a failure of automation. It is the system correctly expressing uncertainty.
Known archetypes, deterministic rules, automated tests, architecture policies, semantic dependency information and AI reasoning can collectively provide evidence for a decision. Where that evidence is strong, the system can progress with greater autonomy. Where it is incomplete, contradictory or unusual, humans become involved because their judgement actually adds value.
This is the same principle that applies more broadly to agentic systems: use deterministic automation where the answer is known, reasoning where interpretation is required, and human judgement where accountability or genuine ambiguity remains.
Modernisation becomes an adaptive flow # Seen this way, AI changes modernisation in a more interesting way than simply making developers faster.
We can begin to model the estate, model the migration routes through it and model the decisions required to move applications between states. Agents can discover, classify, reason and act against that model, while deterministic automation handles the repeatable transformations and validations that we already understand well.
As the programme progresses, the system can learn more about the estate. New archetypes can emerge. Migration patterns can be refined. Exceptions encountered in one application can inform how the next hundred are assessed. The enterprise model becomes richer rather than each migration beginning again with an empty context window.
That is where I think the opportunity starts to become much larger than AI-assisted coding.
The goal is not a machine that can rewrite every application in the estate. It is a modernisation system that understands what should change, why it should change, which path it should follow, when it is safe to change, what constraints surround that change and where human judgement still matters.
If we already use value-stream mapping to understand deployment and continuous delivery, we should apply the same discipline to modernisation. The difference is that the modernisation value stream has to account for much more than the software change itself: dependencies, sequencing, temporary architecture, environments, testing, decision rights and confidence.
AI can accelerate the flow dramatically.
But the real advantage comes when we can also explain why the flow is safe to accelerate.
That is the point at which modernisation starts to become not only faster, but genuinely scalable.
summary:
There is a growing assumption in software modernisation that AI will allow us to industrialise the analysis and transformation of existing estates. Give a model a codebase, define the target architecture and increasingly it can analyse, refactor, generate tests and produce a substantial amount of the target implementation.
There is clearly value in that, but the idea becomes much harder when we move from an individual application to an enterprise estate. The problem is not simply that organisations use different technologies. There can be enormous variation between two applications built in the same language, by the same organisation and notionally against the same standards. Years of design decisions, local conventions, framework choices, technical debt, developer preferences and changing architectural standards leave each application carrying part of its own history.
title: Scaling AI Modernisation Means Scaling Decisions, Not Just Code

content:
Yesterday I wrote about grace as receiving what we do not deserve. But there is another part of grace that I think is easy to miss: grace is only as meaningful as the authority of the person giving it.
At the end of my university years I had accumulated a lot of debt. Some of it was simply the cost of living and studying; some of it, if I am honest, was not always spent particularly wisely. Either way, it was thousands and thousands of pounds, and it was mine. I had incurred it and there was no reasonable argument that somebody else should carry it for me.
Then the government changed the rules. In a day, a huge amount of that debt was wiped away. I had not suddenly become more deserving, and I had not somehow repaid it without noticing. Someone with the authority to make the decision had simply declared that a large part of what I owed no longer had to be paid.
It is only an analogy, and like any analogy it has limits, but it helped me see something important. The release was an act of undeserved grace, but it was also an exercise of authority. If somebody in the street had stopped me and said, “Don’t worry about it, your debt is forgiven,” it might have been a lovely sentiment, but it would have changed absolutely nothing. They did not own the debt and they had no authority over it. The cancellation mattered because the people making the decision had the authority to make it real.
That matters when we talk about Jesus. We rightly speak about the grace of Christ. The cross is where we receive what we could never earn for ourselves: forgiveness, reconciliation and a standing before God that we do not deserve.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:23–24, NIV
But grace is not powerful simply because it is generous. It is powerful because of who gives it.
If Jesus were only a good man offering forgiveness, the cross might be an extraordinary act of compassion, but it could not change our standing before God. The Gospel makes a much greater claim. The one who went to the cross is also the one who says:
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” — Matthew 28:18, NIV
He is not merely sympathetic to our debt. He is Lord, and He has authority to forgive.
Grace and sovereignty belong together # This is where grace and sovereignty meet. Christ does not simply wish that we were forgiven; He has the authority to forgive. He does not merely hope that death will release us; He has conquered death. He does not simply encourage us towards a better future; He is Lord over that future.
Without grace, sovereignty would terrify us. An all-powerful God before whom we have fallen short would give us every reason to fear. But without sovereignty, grace would comfort us without being able to save us. The wonder of the Gospel is that the one with absolute authority is also the one who chooses to exercise that authority in mercy.
That changes how I think about grace. It is not God looking the other way, pretending the debt never existed or saying that what happened did not matter. It is the sovereign Lord dealing with the debt Himself and then declaring us free.
Paul puts this extraordinary movement into a few lines:
“When you were dead in your sins … God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having cancelled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross.” — Colossians 2:13–14, NIV
The language is striking: the debt is real, the charge stands against us, and then Christ cancels it. Not because we negotiated better terms, managed to prove that it was never really ours, or accumulated enough good behaviour to outweigh it. The one with authority dealt with it.
Who has the final word? # Perhaps this is why grace can still be difficult to accept. We know the debt was real. We remember how some of it was accumulated, and we know the things we would undo if we could. Guilt keeps producing the old account and insisting that we read it again.
But the authority to determine our standing before God does not belong to our guilt; it belongs to Christ. We may still regret what we did. We may need to apologise, repair damage or live with consequences, and grace does not make any of that unreal. Condemnation, though, says that our failure still has the final word over who we are. The Gospel says that Christ does.
That is why Romans 8 begins with such confidence:
“Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, NIV
“No condemnation” is not positive thinking or us talking ourselves into feeling better. It is the consequence of what Christ has done and a declaration we can trust because the one speaking grace is Lord.
Read together # Read:
Romans 3:21–26 — grace and justification; Colossians 2:13–15 — the cancelled debt and the victory of Christ; Matthew 28:16–20 — the authority of Jesus; Romans 8:1–4 — no condemnation in Christ. As you read them, notice that the Bible does not separate Christ’s mercy from His authority. The one who forgives is also the one who reigns.
A question to sit with # When guilt reminds you of something Christ has already forgiven, whose judgement are you treating as final: your own, or His?
Grace does not ask us to deny the debt. It asks us to trust the authority of the one who cancelled it.
Prayer # Lord Jesus, thank You that Your grace is not merely a kind thought or a hopeful promise. You are Lord, and You have the authority to forgive, restore and make us new.
Thank You that You knew the full weight of our debt and chose to carry it at the cross. Help us to repent honestly where we have failed, to make right what we can, and then to trust Your word when You say that there is no condemnation for those who are in You.
When guilt keeps presenting an account You have already dealt with, remind us who has the final word. Thank You that the one who has all authority is also full of grace.
Amen.

Read: Scripture Genesis 5:21–24 NIV , Scripture Hebrews 11:5–6 NIV and Scripture Romans 8:31–39 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 73:23–28 NIV Fear often asks the same question in different ways: What if I am left on my own? What if things change? What if I become weaker? What if I cannot remember what I used to remember, or cannot hold onto everything as tightly as I once did?
The Bible gives a very strong answer: you are not the one doing all the holding. God is holding you.
Romans 8 says:
Scripture Romans 8:38–39 NIV That is a remarkable promise. Not age, weakness, fear, confusion or the future can separate you from the love of God in Christ.
Remember Enoch # Enoch is one of the quieter people in the Bible. We are not given a long account of everything he achieved or every important moment in his life. Instead, Genesis gives us this simple description:
Scripture Genesis 5:24 NIV What a wonderful way to describe a life. Enoch lived for hundreds of years, and the thing Scripture chooses to remember is that he walked with God.
Hebrews picks up his story and tells us that Enoch pleased God through faith. His life was one of continuing trust and relationship. That matters because our value to God is not measured by how much we can still achieve, and a life with God is not made valuable by how busy it is. Sometimes the deepest calling is simply this: keep walking with him.
He Is Holding Your Hand # Psalm 73 gives us a beautiful picture:
Scripture Psalm 73:23 NIV Notice who is doing the holding. God is.
There may be days when your own grip feels strong and days when it feels weak. There may be days when prayer comes easily and days when it does not, and days when your thoughts feel clear and days when they feel muddled. But God’s grip does not weaken when yours does. He holds you by the hand.
You Are Still His # Romans 8 does not say that nothing can separate us from God as long as we are strong enough, clear enough or faithful enough. It points us back to Christ.
Your security rests in him. Jesus has already acted for you. He has loved you, called you and made you his own.
So when fear speaks, you can answer it with what is true:
“What if I lose my way?” God knows where I am. “What if I cannot hold on?” God is holding me. “What if I am forgotten?” Nothing can separate me from his love. Read Psalm 73 # Read the final part of the Psalm slowly. The writer talks honestly about weakness:
Scripture Psalm 73:26 NIV That is not a denial of frailty. It is confidence in the middle of frailty. Our bodies change, our strength changes, and our minds can change, but God does not.
Remember # Enoch’s life was remembered because he walked with God. You have walked with God too, and you are still walking with him now. Perhaps the pace has changed and perhaps the path feels different, but the One beside you has not changed.
Remember:
God has not abandoned you. God has not forgotten you. God is still holding you. God is not finished with you. Nothing can separate you from his love. Say this together # I belong to Jesus. God is with me. God is holding my hand. He has not forgotten me. Nothing can separate me from his love. God is not finished with me. I do not need to be afraid.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you are holding me. Thank you that your love does not depend on my strength, my memory or how I feel today.
When I am afraid of being alone, remind me that you are with me. When I feel weak, remind me that you are the strength of my heart.
Thank you for Enoch and for the simple picture of a life spent walking with you. Help me to keep walking with you today, and thank you that nothing can separate me from your love in Christ Jesus.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

There is a lot being written about AI agents at the moment, and much of the conversation understandably focuses on autonomy: agents that can execute tasks, call tools, communicate with other systems and increasingly operate across whole workflows. I think that risks missing one of the more interesting opportunities, because the real power of agentic systems is not simply that they can act. It is that they can close the loop between information, ownership, decisions and change.
That distinction matters because most organisations already have a significant amount of automation. Workflow engines, APIs, rules engines, integration platforms and orchestration tooling can execute known processes quickly, reliably and repeatedly. AI does not make those capabilities obsolete; in many cases, combining them with AI is considerably more powerful than trying to replace them. A system might use deterministic automation for the things we understand clearly, enterprise knowledge to provide context, an AI reasoning layer to interpret circumstances, and memory to understand how those circumstances have changed over time. Agency then adds something different: the ability to recognise that an intervention is required and actively pursue it.
From knowledge repositories to living organisational context # Consider something relatively mundane: an information-security governance control. Most organisations have policies, standards, regulatory interpretations, architecture decisions and operating procedures spread across numerous repositories. Traditionally, we have attempted to solve this by creating a better library. More recently, we have started putting AI over that library so people can ask questions of it. Both are useful, but neither necessarily solves the underlying problem.
Imagine a new document enters the organisation and appears to contradict the currently accepted interpretation of a regulatory requirement. One response is to ignore it until somebody notices. Another is to allow only explicitly curated information into the enterprise knowledge model. That protects quality, but creates a different weakness: the organisation’s understanding is only as current as its manual curation process.
There is another possibility. The system can recognise the contradiction and, because the enterprise context contains not just information but also ownership, identify which person or role is accountable for that area. It can compare the new information with the current organisational understanding, summarise the delta, assemble the relevant evidence and put the issue directly in front of the knowledge owner.
That interaction might happen through a governance portal for something formal, through email where an audit trail is important, or through Teams or Slack where a lighter interaction is sufficient. The communication channel is not the interesting part. What matters is that the system can understand what has changed, what existing knowledge might be affected, who owns that knowledge, what decision is required and what should happen once that decision has been made. That starts to look considerably more powerful than document management or even enterprise search.
Knowledge needs to be maintained, not merely retrieved # This is one of the reasons I think enterprise knowledge graphs and ontologies become increasingly important as organisations move further into AI. It is not enough to hydrate a graph once and treat it as a static representation of the organisation because businesses change continuously: people move roles, regulations evolve, contracts change, markets move and even the interpretation of existing information changes over time.
If AI systems are going to reason against enterprise context, the quality and currency of that context becomes a form of critical infrastructure. That suggests an interesting class of agent: agents whose role is to maintain the context used by other agents and systems. They do not necessarily make business decisions themselves; instead, they can continually identify inconsistencies, stale knowledge, missing ownership, conflicting evidence or changes in the underlying sources from which the organisation’s understanding has been derived.
Where confidence is high and policy permits it, some changes might be applied automatically. Where judgement or accountability is required, the system can escalate to the appropriate owner with the relevant context already assembled. This is also where the combination of deterministic systems and AI becomes important. I would not want an AI model arbitrarily rewriting an organisation’s governance position because it has discovered a new PDF, but I might be very comfortable with an AI system identifying the potential contradiction, locating the accountable owner, explaining the delta and asking for a structured decision. Once that decision is made, deterministic automation can apply it consistently.
Agency does not remove accountability # There is an important architectural and organisational principle underneath this: agency should not mean removing humans from a system. It should mean being much more deliberate about where humans are actually required. There are activities where AI can act autonomously, many where deterministic automation remains the better answer, others where AI can prepare a decision but a human should retain authority, and still more where organisations decide that AI should not participate at all.
The more interesting design question therefore becomes less “Can an agent do this?” and more “Where should the decision right sit, and what information does each actor need in order to exercise it well?” That is not purely a technology question; it is an operating-model question as well. It also builds on the distinction between human presence and genuine human judgement I explored in Human in the loop isn’t the same as human judgement.
It also connects directly to the wider conversation about controls and guardrails. The objective should not be to insert a human into every step simply because doing so feels safer, nor should we assume that removing humans creates a better system. The aim is to place judgement where judgement has value, deterministic controls where the answer is known, and agency where the system benefits from being able to recognise and pursue change.
Compressing organisational latency # The business value becomes clearer when you think about all of this in terms of latency. In a traditional organisation, somebody may discover new information, realise that it conflicts with an existing policy, find the right team, identify the appropriate SME, arrange a conversation, explain the context and eventually trigger a change. Depending on the organisation, that can take days, weeks or occasionally months.
An intelligent system can compress much of that journey, not because it necessarily makes the final decision, but because it can recognise the event, identify the relevant owner, assemble the context and put the decision in front of them within minutes. For regulatory policy, that degree of speed may not always matter. For other areas it can matter a great deal: a shift in market conditions, a new commercial opportunity, a changing supply constraint, a new contract structure or a change in a customer’s risk profile can all create situations where the value lies partly in how quickly the organisation recognises the change and responds.
The same pattern applies in each case: detect the change, understand it in the context of the enterprise, identify ownership, determine whether existing rules still apply, engage the appropriate decision-maker where required, update the enterprise context and allow the systems operating against that context to adapt.
From automation to an adaptive enterprise # This is why I think some of the most powerful applications of agentic AI will look less like isolated assistants and more like an organisational nervous system. The deterministic systems remain, as do the APIs and workflows, but around them we can create a contextual layer capable of understanding the enterprise, recognising change and directing attention towards the places where decisions need to be made.
Memory allows that system to understand how its context has evolved over time. Knowledge graphs make relationships and ownership explicit. Reasoning helps interpret ambiguity. Agents provide the ability to act, while deterministic automation gives us reliability where the required behaviour is already understood. None of those components is particularly revolutionary in isolation; the interesting part is what happens when they are combined.
The organisations that get this right may find that the biggest benefit of AI is not simply doing today’s work faster. It is reducing the time between the world changing and the organisation understanding what it needs to do about it. That, to me, is a much more interesting definition of an agentic enterprise.
summary: There is a lot being written about AI agents at the moment, and much of the conversation understandably focuses on autonomy: agents that can execute tasks, call tools, communicate with other systems and increasingly operate across whole workflows. I think that risks missing one of the more interesting opportunities, because the real power of agentic systems is not simply that they can act. It is that they can close the loop between information, ownership, decisions and change.
title: The Real Power of Agentic Systems Is Closing the Loop

I’ve worked across quite different spaces: large organisations, charities, churches and smaller entrepreneurial settings. Different language, different structures and different motivations, but three activities keep showing up: governance, leadership and management.
We often use those words almost interchangeably. A senior manager gets called a leader. A trustee gets involved in operations because they are accountable. A founder moves between vision, people and tasks without really noticing. Sometimes that flexibility is necessary; sometimes it quietly creates confusion.
I became particularly conscious of this when I was running my own business. We had brought in agile coaching to help the team grow its own decision-making capability, yet I noticed that I could walk into the room and the dynamic would shift. I did not need to take over, or even intend to influence the conversation. My presence changed its weight.
That was uncomfortable because my intention might simply have been to help, but intention was not really the point. My role gave anything I said a different gravity. The tension between accountability and responsibility looks clean on paper and feels far less clear in the moment.
Doing the right things, and doing things right # Peter Drucker’s distinction between effectiveness and efficiency has stayed useful to me here. His formulation is simple: “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.”
That does not map perfectly onto governance, leadership and management, and I do not think it should. But it does give me a useful way into the distinction.
Governance asks whether we are doing the right things, within appropriate boundaries, with clear accountability. Leadership gives direction: where are we going, why does it matter, and what are we trying to become? Management organises the activity, capability and resources that help us get there. All three matter. None is inherently superior, but they are not the same job.
Drucker also wrote extensively about contribution and responsibility. That matters because governance is not simply an exercise in control, and leadership is not simply having the loudest voice in the room. Both should create the conditions for other people to make a meaningful contribution rather than quietly pulling every decision back towards the centre.
That is easy to agree with in principle. It is harder when something important is not being done.
When the lines bend # I have found this particularly difficult in charity governance. There have been times when I have taken on a leadership or trustee role and could immediately see operational things that simply were not being done. Standing back because something is “not my role” sounds disciplined until an important responsibility is falling through a gap.
I have not always judged that boundary well. The instinct to dive in is strong, particularly when you know you can solve the immediate problem. Looking back, that behaviour feels remarkably similar to founder mode: carry whatever needs carrying because the capability does not yet exist elsewhere.
Perhaps the important thing is to recognise that for what it is: a season of constraint, rather than the model we are aiming for.
Constraints are real. They should influence the choices we make today, but they should not quietly define our horizon. If I continually compensate for missing capability by doing the work myself, I may solve the immediate problem while also removing the pressure, space or opportunity for that capability to develop elsewhere.
Stephen Covey’s Begin With the End in Mind is useful here. The current constraint matters, but it is not the destination. If we allow every decision to be driven by what is urgent today, we can become remarkably effective at preserving the organisation we already have rather than building the one we actually need.
That is where accountability becomes interesting. Being accountable for an outcome does not necessarily mean being responsible for performing every activity that produces it.
Founder mode appears in more places than startups # The founder case makes the overlap obvious. Early in a business, one person may genuinely govern, lead, manage and do. Trying to create pristine boundaries too early can be artificial and may slow down the thing you are trying to build.
But founder mode is not limited to founders.
It can appear when taking over a struggling function, starting a new team, rebuilding a charity activity or planting a church. A gap exists between the organisation we currently have and the organisation required to carry the vision, so a small number of people stretch across that gap.
For a period, that can be exactly what progress requires. The danger comes when the temporary response becomes permanent. What was once fuel becomes friction, because the organisation never develops beyond the capability and availability of the people who started it.
J. Oswald Sanders approaches the same problem from the perspective of spiritual leadership. In Spiritual Leadership, his treatment of delegation is not simply about passing out tasks. Responsibility and authority have to travel together. If I tell somebody they are responsible for an outcome but continue to pull the real authority back towards myself, I have not delegated as much as I think I have.
That takes me straight back to that room with the agile coaches.
I could tell the team that a decision was theirs. I could genuinely mean it. But if my presence as founder changed what people were willing to say, or caused everyone to wait for my view, then the formal allocation of responsibility only told part of the story.
Authority has a gravitational effect.
Church contexts make this more layered still. Trustees, elders, employed leaders and volunteers can all hold different forms of responsibility and authority. Formal reporting lines only tell part of the story because informal and spiritual influence can carry at least as much weight as organisational authority.
That does not mean leaders should stand back. It means we need to notice what our presence does to other people’s responsibility, and whether the structures around us allow people to grow into the authority we say we have given them.
Which hat am I wearing? # I have become more conscious of this in myself. Sometimes I am setting direction. Sometimes I am protecting a boundary or asking whether we are operating responsibly. Sometimes I am mentoring, structuring work or helping someone develop. Sometimes there is simply something practical that needs to be done.
The challenge is not the variety. It is remembering which hat I am wearing, and recognising that the hat I think I am wearing may not be the one everybody else sees.
That matters because a suggestion from a peer is not always heard in the same way when it comes from a founder, trustee, director or senior leader. Even when we deliberately leave a decision with somebody else, our involvement can unintentionally make it feel as though the decision has already been made.
So perhaps the aim is not perfectly separated boxes. It is clarity about:
who is accountable; who is setting direction; who has decision authority; who is organising the work; and who is actually responsible for doing it. In smaller or growing settings those lines may cross frequently, but if that crossing is a response to constraint, we need to recognise it as such.
Covey’s language of beginning with the end in mind helps me again here. The constraint we live with today should influence what we do today. It should not become the limit of what we believe is possible tomorrow.
That leaves me with a question I want to ask myself more often:
What role am I actually performing right now, and what happens to somebody else’s responsibility when I step into it?
That is probably the right place for the next reflection to begin.
summary:
I’ve worked across quite different spaces: large organisations, charities, churches and smaller entrepreneurial settings. Different language, different structures and different motivations, but three activities keep showing up: governance, leadership and management.
We often use those words almost interchangeably. A senior manager gets called a leader. A trustee gets involved in operations because they are accountable. A founder moves between vision, people and tasks without really noticing. Sometimes that flexibility is necessary; sometimes it quietly creates confusion.
title: Governance, Leadership and Management

content:
When we talk about grace, it can become one of those Christian words that we understand without always feeling the full weight of it. We know the definition: unmerited favour. Something given to us that we have not earned and do not deserve.
Perhaps the easiest way to understand grace is to remember what it feels like to receive an unexpected gift, particularly when you were expecting something very different.
When I was younger, I spent quite a lot of energy trying to be like the people around me. I could drink as hard as they could, party as hard as they could and generally try to prove that I could keep up. Some of it was fun, and some of the memories still make me smile, but there is always a cost.
As I got older, there were things I could look back on and know were simply not God’s path for me. Choices I would not make again. Moments where, however much I might explain the circumstances or point out that everyone around me was doing much the same thing, I knew better.
That is one of the difficult things about guilt. It is remarkably resistant to explanation. You can tell yourself you were young, point to the people you were with, or say that it happened years ago and surely you should have moved on by now. Yet somewhere underneath all of that remains a simple truth: I knew this was not right.
Scripture does not try to talk us out of that feeling by pretending we have done nothing wrong. Quite the opposite.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God…”
— Romans 3:23, NIV
That is not particularly comforting if we stop there. We have all fallen short. Not some unusually bad group of people somewhere else. Not simply those whose failures are more visible than ours. All of us.
But Paul does not stop there either.
“…and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.”
— Romans 3:24, NIV
Those two verses belong together: we have fallen short, and we are justified freely.
That is grace.
The answer to guilt is not convincing myself that I did nothing wrong. It is discovering that Jesus already knew I had, and grace was offered anyway.
Most of us understand transactions. If I do something good, perhaps I deserve something good in return. If I work hard, I expect to be rewarded. If I cause damage, I expect to pay for it.
Grace breaks the transaction.
Instead:
we prepare ourselves for the bill and receive a gift; we expect rejection and find ourselves welcomed; we prepare our defence and discover that the Father is already coming towards us. Jesus paints exactly that picture in the story of the prodigal son. The younger son has taken his inheritance, left home and wasted it. Eventually he comes to his senses and heads back to his father with a speech prepared.
“Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”
— Luke 15:21, NIV
He is right about one thing: he has done wrong. The father never tells him otherwise.
But the son has also worked out what he thinks should happen next. He knows he has forfeited his position and expects that perhaps he can negotiate his way back into the household as a servant.
The father refuses the calculation.
He calls for:
the best robe; a ring on his finger; sandals on his feet; a feast. The son returns expecting to negotiate for employment and discovers that his father is restoring him as a son.
That is the scandal of grace. It is not that our sin suddenly becomes insignificant. It is that God’s mercy is greater, and grace gives us a status we could never earn.
Paul later writes:
“Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
— Romans 8:1, NIV
No condemnation does not mean there is nothing in our lives to regret. There may be choices we would desperately like to make differently, and there may be consequences that cannot simply be undone. Grace does not require us to rewrite our history until everything we did becomes acceptable.
Instead, it allows us to look honestly at our history without being imprisoned by it.
I can say, I was wrong, without needing to add, and therefore I am forever condemned, because Christ has already answered the second part.
Perhaps that is why grace is such a powerful antidote to guilt. Guilt continually drags us back into the courtroom and asks us to argue the case again. Grace points us towards a judgement that has already been dealt with at the cross.
Grace does something else too. It does not simply forgive the person we were and leave us exactly as we are.
Paul writes:
“For the grace of God has appeared that offers salvation to all people. It teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions…”
— Titus 2:11–12, NIV
The same grace that releases us from our past begins to shape our future. We do not change in order to earn grace; we change because we have received it.
That difference matters.
If my relationship with God depends upon continually proving that I deserve to be there, then every failure becomes a threat. I have to hide it, minimise it or somehow compensate for it. But if I understand grace, I can bring failure into the light. I can repent honestly, learn and change, not because the Father is standing at a distance deciding whether I have finally earned my way home, but because He has already run down the road to meet me.
Perhaps some of us are still carrying things from years ago: decisions we made, relationships we damaged, seasons where we wandered much further than we intended. We know the cost, and we know we fell short.
The extraordinary joy of the Gospel is that God knows too.
And then He gives us exactly what we do not deserve:
mercy; forgiveness; welcome; a place at the table; the status of a son or daughter. That is grace.
Read together # Read Romans 3:21–26, then Luke 15:11–24, paying particular attention to what the son expects to receive and what the father actually gives him.
A question to sit with # Is there something from your past that you have confessed to God, but are still trying to punish yourself for?
Grace does not ask you to pretend it did not matter. It asks you to believe that what Jesus did matters more.
Prayer # Father, thank You for grace.
Thank You that You do not ask us to pretend we have never failed, and that You already know the parts of our story we would rather forget. Forgive us for the times we have walked away from Your path, and help us to repent honestly while also receiving the forgiveness You freely give.
When guilt tries to pull us back into something You have already forgiven, remind us that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Teach us to live differently, not because we are trying to earn Your love, but because we have already received it.
Thank You for giving us what we could never deserve.
Amen.
summary:
When we talk about grace, it can become one of those Christian words that we understand without always feeling the full weight of it. We know the definition: unmerited favour. Something given to us that we have not earned and do not deserve.
Perhaps the easiest way to understand grace is to remember what it feels like to receive an unexpected gift, particularly when you were expecting something very different.
title: Grace: What We Don't Deserve
