I had a conversation with a client recently that crystallised something I have been thinking about for a while.
Like many organisations, they are asking reasonable questions about the value they are getting from AI. There has been plenty of experimentation and no shortage of potential use cases, but the return still feels smaller than the scale of the conversation.
What struck me was how the work was being described. AI was one thing. Digital transformation was another. Service transformation sat somewhere else again.
I left the conversation thinking that those two observations may be connected.
AI beside the critical path # A lot of current enterprise AI adoption sits beside the critical path. It helps somebody draft an email, summarise a document, search for information, prepare a response or create a first version of something that would otherwise be produced manually.
Those things are useful. Saving time repeatedly across a large workforce matters, and better access to information can remove genuine friction. But in many cases the service itself has not changed.
The customer still makes the same request. It still enters the same queue, crosses the same hand-offs and waits for the same approvals. The same organisational boundaries still determine how quickly the work progresses.
We have made somebody standing beside the process faster without necessarily making the process flow any better.
A simple way to see the problem is that AI is often helping the people around the flow while leaving the flow itself unchanged.
flowchart LR C[Customer request] --> A[Team A] A --> Q1[Queue] Q1 --> B[Team B] B --> AP[Approval] AP --> S[Service outcome] AI1[AI helps draft / summarise / search] -.-> A AI2[AI helps prepare / interpret] -.-> BThis is where I think some of the disappointment around AI ROI becomes understandable.
Imagine a request that spends two days waiting for approval. AI reduces the time needed to prepare the approval pack from ten minutes to thirty seconds. That is a real improvement, but the request still waits two days.
The more interesting question is why it waits.
Perhaps somebody has to gather information from several systems, understand the request, compare it with policy, assess risk and decide whether an exception is acceptable. Once you look at the whole decision, a different set of questions appears:
Could the context be assembled automatically? Could explicit policy handle the obvious cases? Could deterministic automation perform the predictable actions? Could AI identify ambiguity and assemble the evidence needed for a decision? Could only genuinely exceptional cases reach a person? At that point we are no longer asking how AI helps someone complete the approval faster. We are asking whether the approval needs to exist in its current form at all.
We may not have an AI ROI problem. We may have an AI placement problem.
Beside the path may be the right place to start # There is an important qualification here.
I do not think organisations should rush to put AI onto the critical path simply because that is where the larger value might be. Keeping AI beside the flow can be exactly the right place to begin.
It gives teams room to learn what the models are good at, where they fail, what context they need and how people actually use them. It allows trust, controls and operational understanding to develop before the capability is allowed to influence important decisions or actions.
The problem is not augmentation. The problem is mistaking a sensible learning phase for the destination.
If the AI remains permanently outside the service, then the organisation should be realistic about the economics it is likely to change. A tool that makes one activity faster can be valuable, but it is unlikely by itself to transform a service whose performance is dominated by queues, dependencies, approvals or poor decision design.
That feels especially important when AI has its own programme, its own roadmap and its own portfolio of use cases. The organisational structure can quietly reinforce the technical one: AI becomes something to add to existing work rather than something that helps us reconsider how the work should operate.
Redesigning the path # Putting AI into the critical path does not mean handing the service over to an LLM. The more interesting architecture combines different capabilities.
Some decisions are better expressed as deterministic rules. Some actions belong in established workflow or automation platforms. Some situations require genuine human judgement. AI is useful where it can interpret demand, assemble context, reason across ambiguity and help decide which of those capabilities should be invoked.
flowchart TD CR[Customer request] --> ID[Interpret demand] ID --> CTX[Gather enterprise context] CTX --> POL{Clear policy / rules?} POL -->|Yes| AUTO[Deterministic automation] POL -->|No| AI[AI reasoning and recommendation] AI --> EX{Genuine exception or judgement needed?} EX -->|No| AUTO EX -->|Yes| HJ[Human judgement] AUTO --> OUT[Service outcome] HJ --> OUTThe point is not that AI replaces the service. It is that the existence of these capabilities changes the design space.
The progression is not simply manual work → AI work. It is closer to understand the flow → identify the constraints and decisions → redesign the service using the right combination of AI, automation, policy and human judgement.
That also changes what we should measure. Adoption numbers tell us whether people are using the tools; they do not tell us whether the system improved. I am much more interested in questions such as:
Has lead time changed? Has a queue disappeared? Have hand-offs reduced? Can more requests be resolved at first contact? Can the service handle more demand without simply adding people? Those are not particularly novel AI metrics. They are measures of whether the service itself became better.
The organisational question # This brings me back to the client conversation.
If AI is one programme, Digital is redesigning customer journeys, Service is improving operations and the business has its own transformation agenda, who owns the redesign of the complete value stream?
Dedicated AI capability is useful while organisations build skills, platforms, controls and common patterns. But if AI remains permanently separated from service design, architecture and operating-model change, its organisational placement may limit the problems it is able to see.
If an AI team is asked to find AI use cases, it will find AI use cases. If a service team is asked to improve flow, it may discover that AI is part of the answer alongside policy changes, automation, removing approvals or changing where decisions sit.
Those are very different starting points.
So I am increasingly less interested in the question “Where can we use AI?”
I would rather take one important service, draw the path from demand to outcome, mark the queues, decisions, hand-offs and constraints, and then ask:
How should this service work now that these capabilities exist?
If most of the AI investment still sits beside that path, there may be good reasons for it. But we should not be surprised if the returns are incremental too.
The opportunity is not simply to put AI on the critical path. It is to use AI, automation and human judgement to ask whether the critical path should still look like that at all.

Read: Scripture Romans 4:16–21 NIV and Scripture Galatians 3:26–29 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 105:1–11 NIV There are moments when it helps to remember not only who we are, but whose we are.
Life changes. Our strength changes. Our responsibilities change. Sometimes even the way we see ourselves can change. But if you belong to Jesus, there is something deeper than all of that.
You belong to God.
You are part of his family. You are part of a story that began long before you were born and will continue long after your own lifetime.
Remember Abraham # Abraham learned to live by promise.
God had spoken to him years earlier and promised that his family would become something far greater than Abraham could yet see. But time passed. Abraham became older. Sarah became older. The promise looked less and less likely from a human point of view.
Romans says:
Scripture Romans 4:18 NIV Abraham did not have confidence because everything around him looked easy. He had confidence because God had spoken.
And God had not forgotten his promise.
That matters because the New Testament tells us that the story of Abraham does not end with Abraham.
Paul writes:
Scripture Galatians 3:29 NIV That means this story includes you.
You Belong to a Bigger Story # Your faith did not begin with you.
For generations, people have trusted God, prayed, worshipped, struggled, hoped, failed, started again and discovered that God remained faithful.
You are part of that same story.
That is part of your heritage in Christ.
There may be things about your own past that become harder to remember, but your place in God’s family does not depend on your ability to remember every detail.
You are still his.
You are still loved.
You are still an heir through Christ.
Read Psalm 105 # Psalm 105 begins with an invitation:
Scripture Psalm 105:1 NIV Then it tells God’s people to remember.
Scripture Psalm 105:5 NIV The Psalm looks back over generations of God’s faithfulness. It reminds the people that they are not standing alone in the present moment. They are part of a covenant story.
That is important when the present feels uncertain.
Sometimes the best way to face today is to remember that God has been faithful before.
He was faithful to Abraham.
He was faithful to generations after him.
And he has been faithful to you.
Your Inheritance Is Secure # Galatians says:
Scripture Galatians 3:26 NIV That is not something age can take away.
It is not something weakness can take away.
It is not something fear can take away.
And it is not something confusion can take away.
You belong to God because of what Christ has done, not because of how strong you feel today.
Your inheritance rests in him.
You Still Have a Place in the Story # Heritage is not only about looking backwards.
It is also about what we pass on.
You still have something to give.
You can still pray.
You can still speak about God’s faithfulness.
You can still bless your family.
You can still encourage someone younger.
You can still remind the next generation that God has been good.
The story is not finished with you.
Remember # I belong to Jesus.
I am part of God’s family.
I am part of a story of faith.
God has kept his promises before.
He has not forgotten me.
He is not finished with me.
Say this together # I belong to God.
I am his child.
I am part of his family.
God has been faithful.
God is faithful now.
God will remain faithful.
I do not need to be afraid.
Prayer # Father, thank you that I belong to you.
Thank you that my life is part of a much bigger story of faith and promise. Thank you for Abraham and for every generation that has trusted you before me.
When I feel uncertain, help me remember that your promises are not uncertain. When I forget things, remind me that you have not forgotten me.
Thank you that through Jesus I am your child and an heir of your promise.
Help me to keep trusting you and to pass on what I know of your faithfulness to those who come after me.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Read: Scripture Genesis 12:1–4 NIV and Scripture Genesis 17:1–7 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 139:1–18 NIV There can be something unsettling about feeling less certain of yourself than you once did. Names can become harder to remember. Familiar things can sometimes feel unfamiliar. Even our own story can become more difficult to hold together.
But God does not know us in the uncertain way that we sometimes know ourselves. He knows us completely.
Psalm 139 says:
Scripture Psalm 139:1 NIV God knows where you are. He knows what you are thinking. He knows the things you can explain and the things you cannot. He knows your past, your present and everything still ahead of you.
And he knows your name.
Remember Abraham # When God first called Abraham, Abraham was already seventy-five years old.
God said:
Scripture Genesis 12:1 NIV It would have been easy to imagine that the significant chapters of Abraham’s life were already behind him. But God did not look at Abraham’s age and say, “It is too late.”
Instead, God called him forward.
Years later, when Abraham was ninety-nine, God spoke to him again. He renewed his promise and even gave him a new name. Abram became Abraham.
God was still speaking. Still leading. Still promising. Still working.
God was not finished with Abraham.
And what God was doing in Abraham’s life was bigger than Abraham could yet see. His life was becoming part of a story that would continue through generations.
God Knows Your Story # Psalm 139 says:
Scripture Psalm 139:16 NIV There are parts of your story you may remember very clearly and parts that may become harder to recall. But God has not forgotten any of it.
He remembers the prayers you have prayed, the people you have loved, the times you trusted him, the things you have learned and the ways you have served. None of that is lost to him.
Your life is not held together by your ability to remember every detail.
Your life is held by God.
You Are Known # Sometimes fear tells us that because things are changing, we are somehow becoming lost.
But you are not lost to God.
The same God who knew Abraham, called Abraham and continued working in Abraham’s life knows you too. He is not confused about who you are. He has not misplaced you. He has not forgotten your place in his family.
You belong to him.
And because you belong to Jesus, your identity is deeper than memory, age or circumstance.
Read Psalm 139 # Read it slowly.
Notice how often David comes back to the same truth: God knows me. God sees me. God is with me.
Scripture Psalm 139:7 NIV The answer is nowhere.
There is nowhere you can go where God stops knowing you. There is no season of life where he loses sight of you.
Remember # God knows my name.
God knows my story.
God has not forgotten me.
I belong to Jesus.
God is still at work in me.
Abraham discovered that some of the most important parts of his story came much later than he expected.
Your age does not make you invisible to God.
Your weakness does not make you less loved.
And change does not mean God is finished with you.
Say this together # God knows me.
God knows my name.
I belong to Jesus.
God has not forgotten me.
He is still with me.
He is still at work in me.
I do not need to be afraid.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you know me completely.
Thank you that you know my name and every part of my story. When things feel uncertain, help me remember that I am not uncertain to you.
Thank you for Abraham and for the reminder that you continued to call him, lead him and work through him even in later life.
Help me to trust that you are still with me and still at work in me.
When I am afraid, remind me that I belong to you.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

I have been working with a couple of teams recently where, despite the problems being quite different, I keep seeing the same behaviour.
They are looking at their toes.
In one case, it is a technical team dealing with a standard security-related change process. There is a substantial amount of work in flight, different kinds of requests are mixed together, and the team is struggling to see what is actually happening across the system. Work enters, progresses through a series of activities and approvals, gets delayed, is picked up again, and eventually comes out the other side. Everyone is busy, but it is remarkably difficult to answer some fairly basic questions: what is holding things up, which work is genuinely complex, where is the constraint, and what could we change to make the whole thing flow better?
The image that keeps coming to mind is an old manufacturing floor where work-in-progress has been allowed to accumulate between workstations. Eventually there is so much inventory piled up that you cannot even see the next workstation. The work itself obscures the system.
That feels very similar to what happens in overloaded technology teams. When there are enough tickets, escalations, meetings, exceptions and urgent requests in front of you, your field of vision gradually gets shorter. You stop looking at how the system works because almost all of your energy is consumed by moving the next thing. Strangely, the harder everyone works, the harder it can become to see how to make the work easier.
Looking down can be a perfectly rational response # The second example looks quite different. I am working with an organisation dealing with a highly regulated, manually intensive process. Some of the decisions involved have significant contractual consequences and can affect investments worth millions of pounds. There has previously been considerable scrutiny around how parts of the process were handled, so accuracy, control and evidence understandably matter.
The reaction has been to become extremely careful, and that reaction makes sense. If you have tripped over, the natural response is to watch where you put your feet next. If an organisation has made mistakes, particularly visible or expensive ones, increased scrutiny is not irrational. People check more things. Decisions are escalated. Evidence is gathered. Processes become tighter.
The problem comes when a short-term protective behaviour becomes the long-term operating model.
Looking at your toes is a great way to make sure you do not trip over the thing immediately in front of you. But if you continue looking at your toes, you will never see where you are going. You certainly will not run.
There is something interesting in that analogy. As children learn to move confidently, they gradually stop concentrating entirely on every individual step. Running requires us to look further ahead. We are constantly processing the terrain in front of us, but our attention has moved towards where we are trying to get to. Organisations need to do something similar. That does not mean ignoring immediate risks. It means becoming capable enough at dealing with the immediate terrain that we regain the ability to look towards the horizon.
Stress shortens the horizon # I have written before about the importance of borrowing horizons: about asking not simply how we make today’s process slightly better, but what might become possible if we reconsider some of its assumptions. There is another side to that idea.
Sometimes teams do not lack ambition. They lack the capacity required to exercise it.
When an organisation is under sustained pressure, its planning horizon contracts. The immediate problem becomes dominant. The overdue request, the next regulatory response, today’s incident, the thing somebody senior has just escalated — these consume attention because there is rarely enough capacity remaining to think about what would stop the same situation happening again.
That is why telling an overloaded team to “be more strategic” is often fairly useless advice. Strategy requires some distance from the immediate problem. You need enough space to observe patterns, challenge assumptions and imagine alternatives. You need time to ask why ten apparently different problems keep occurring at the same point in the process. You need enough cognitive room to notice that something everyone accepts as inevitable may simply be the consequence of how the system has been designed. If every available moment is already consumed by execution, that capacity disappears.
Busyness has a nonlinear cost # This is one reason Tom DeMarco’s Slack has stayed with me. One of its central challenges is to the idea that maximum efficiency makes an organisation more responsive. In reality, removing all spare capacity can have precisely the opposite effect.
Queueing theory gives us a useful way of understanding why. As utilisation rises, waiting time does not rise neatly alongside it. As a resource approaches full utilisation, relatively small increases in demand can produce disproportionately large increases in queues and response times.
At 50% utilisation, there is usually capacity available to absorb the next piece of work. At 80 or 90%, the probability that new work arrives while existing work is still being handled becomes much greater. Push towards 100% and almost every piece of incoming work has to wait behind something else.
This is an abstraction, of course. People are not servers and technology teams are not mathematically tidy queues. But the behaviour is recognisable. It explains the team where everyone appears incredibly busy but nothing seems to move quickly. It explains why something genuinely urgent creates chaos rather than simply being absorbed. And it explains why overloaded teams struggle so much with improvement: the spare capacity we sometimes dismiss as inefficiency is often precisely the capacity that would allow somebody to understand why the system keeps creating the work in the first place.
Slack is not necessarily unused capacity. Sometimes it is thinking capacity.
The horizon cannot belong only to the leader # There is an obvious counterargument here: surely looking towards the horizon is the leader’s job. To an extent, yes. Leadership should provide direction, create context and help people understand where they are trying to go. There is also a difference between leadership and management, although that is probably a different article.
But I do not think the future view should exist only at the top of an organisation. Some of the best observations about how a system could work differently come from the people closest to it. They see the repeated exception. They know which approval adds little value. They notice that three requests which look identical on a dashboard require completely different levels of effort. They know which workaround everybody quietly performs because the formal process does not quite work.
These people may not carry the title of leader, but they influence how teams think and how systems evolve. The danger is that persistent overload suppresses those voices. If somebody is permanently trying to catch up, there is little opportunity to develop an idea about how the process might change. If an organisation has created an environment where making a mistake is more visible than improving the system, people will naturally optimise for not being wrong. If every conversation starts with what has gone wrong this week, eventually people stop bringing ideas about what might be possible next year.
We then lose much more than capacity. We lose the best thinking of the people inside the system.
Controls can reinforce the problem # This is also where my thinking about human judgement, controls and guardrails connects. When something goes wrong, organisations understandably add controls: an additional check, another approval, more evidence, another person who must confirm that a decision is correct. Some of those controls may be essential.
But every control also consumes capacity, adds another potential queue and reinforces attention on the immediate step. If we are not careful, a system designed to prevent yesterday’s mistake gradually removes the organisation’s ability to design tomorrow’s solution.
The question therefore cannot simply be How do we stop this happening again? It also needs to be What would allow this system to operate differently? Those are subtly different questions. One looks primarily backwards. The other preserves the learning from what happened while still allowing us to look forwards.
That is why good guardrails are so powerful. Where rules can be made explicit, automated and embedded into the system, they can provide safety without demanding constant human attention. Human judgement can then be concentrated on the places where judgement genuinely adds value rather than consuming people’s time proving repeatedly that routine decisions remain routine.
We protect our feet without requiring everyone to stare at them.
Sometimes the first intervention is simply visibility # Going back to the security-related change example, I am not convinced the first answer is a major technology transformation. It may simply be seeing the work differently.
What kinds of work are actually entering the system? How large are they? How many dependencies do they carry? Where is work waiting rather than being worked on? Which queues are growing? How old is the work in each queue? Which supposedly standard requests generate most of the exceptions?
Once those distinctions become visible, the conversation changes. Instead of asking how to process an enormous homogeneous backlog faster, we can start identifying different flows. Perhaps some requests can be standardised. Perhaps others can be automated. Perhaps high-complexity work needs a completely different route. Perhaps one approval is the real constraint. Perhaps we discover that the team itself is not the bottleneck at all.
Visibility gives us distance from the individual ticket, and distance gives us the opportunity to think.
Look up # There is a temptation when organisations are under pressure to demand greater focus. Sometimes that is exactly what is needed. But focus can become myopia.
A team can become extraordinarily good at concentrating on the work immediately in front of it while gradually losing sight of why that work exists, how the surrounding system behaves, and where it is ultimately trying to go. That is particularly dangerous because it can look like commitment. Everyone is busy. Everyone is concentrating. Everyone is trying incredibly hard not to make mistakes. Yet the organisation may still be moving slowly, because nobody has enough capacity to look up.
There is value in watching your feet. It stops you tripping over the next obstacle. But at some point you have to raise your eyes.
Because if you spend the entire journey looking at your toes, you may avoid a few stones along the way. You just might not get where you intended to go.

Read: Scripture 1 John 4:4–18 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 56 NIV Fear can be very convincing. It can make a thought feel certain simply because it feels strong. It can make something small feel enormous, or make us feel that because we are frightened, the thing we fear must have power over us.
John writes to believers with a very different perspective:
Scripture 1 John 4:4 NIV That is not a promise that frightening things will never happen. It is a reminder about who is greater. Fear is not greater. Confusion is not greater. The things we cannot explain are not greater. Jesus is greater.
John knew what it was to keep walking with Jesus # By the time John wrote these words, he had followed Jesus for many years. He had seen extraordinary things, but he had also lived through loss, opposition and uncertainty. He had watched friends die, seen the church go through difficulty, and continued to serve Christ into later life.
And he was still writing. Still encouraging. Still reminding believers of what was true.
John’s age did not mean that God was finished with him. His circumstances did not mean that his purpose was over. In later life, one of the things God used him to do was to help others remember the truth when fear and confusion were pressing in.
That matters for us too. God is not finished with you. You can still pray. You can still encourage. You can still speak of God’s faithfulness. You can still love people well. You can still remind the next generation of what God has done.
When I am afraid # Psalm 56 does not pretend that fear is not real. David says plainly:
Scripture Psalm 56:3 NIV Notice that he does not say, “I am never afraid.” He says, when I am afraid.
Faith is not pretending that fear has disappeared. Sometimes faith is simply turning again towards God while the fear is still there. You may not be able to reason your way through every troubling thought, but you can return to what is true: God is here. Jesus is greater. I belong to him.
Later in 1 John 4, John writes that God’s love drives out fear. The more securely we know that we are loved by God, the less authority fear is allowed to have over us. We are not trying to make ourselves safe enough for God to love us. We are already his.
Remember # A frightening thought is still only a thought. A strong feeling is still only a feeling. Neither one changes who God is, and neither one changes who you are in Christ.
The One who lives in you is greater.
And the God who has walked with you through all the years behind you is still with you today. Your story is not finished, your place in his family has not changed, and your life still has purpose.
Say this together # I belong to Jesus. God is with me. God has not forgotten me. Greater is he who is in me. God is not finished with me. When I am afraid, I will trust in him.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you are greater than anything that frightens me. When fear feels strong, help me remember that fear is not in charge. Jesus is greater, and I belong to him.
Thank you for all the years you have walked with me, and thank you that you are still with me today. Help me to trust you, to rest in your love, and to remember that you are still able to use my life to encourage and bless others.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Read: Scripture Joshua 1:1–9 NIV Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
Joshua was facing something enormous. Moses had died, and after years of watching Moses lead Israel, Joshua was now responsible for leading the people into the land God had promised them. Thousands of people were looking to him, there were enemies ahead, and Joshua couldn’t possibly know exactly what was going to happen.
Into that uncertainty, God repeatedly tells him: “Be strong and courageous.”
What does being strong mean? # When you hear the word strong, what do you picture? Someone with enormous muscles? Someone who wins fights? Someone who isn’t frightened of anything? Someone who never cries?
What does being strong mean to you? Who do you know that you would describe as strong, and what makes them strong?
It’s easy to imagine that courage means not being scared. But if Joshua had nothing to fear, God wouldn’t need to keep telling him to be courageous. Joshua had plenty of reasons to be frightened. Courage mattered precisely because what he was being asked to do was difficult. Being courageous isn’t the same as having no fear. Sometimes courage means being afraid and choosing to do what is right anyway.
Where does Joshua’s courage come from? # God doesn’t simply tell Joshua to try harder to be brave. He gives him a reason to be courageous: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you.” Then, at the end of the passage, God says it again: “For the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.”
Joshua’s confidence wasn’t supposed to come from believing that he was strong enough to handle everything. His courage came from knowing who was with him.
Right in the middle of these instructions, though, God also tells Joshua something else: “Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night.” Joshua is told to keep returning to God’s word: to read it, talk about it, think about it and, importantly, do what it says. God’s word wasn’t supposed to be something Joshua occasionally consulted. It was meant to shape how he thought and how he lived.
There’s an important connection here. God tells Joshua to be courageous, reminds him of His presence, and tells him to keep His word continually before him. Joshua would face situations where what he could see gave him plenty of reasons to be afraid. God’s word reminded him of something greater than what he could see.
What about us? # Most of us aren’t preparing to lead a nation into the Promised Land, but we all face things that require courage. It might be something happening at school, a difficult friendship, trying something when you’re worried you’ll fail, standing up for someone, admitting you’ve done something wrong, or simply doing the right thing when everyone around you is doing something different.
So think of something happening in your life right now where you need courage. What would being “strong and courageous” actually look like in that situation? What are you frightened might happen? And what difference does it make to know that God is with you in it?
Perhaps that’s the most important thing to remember from Joshua’s story. Biblical courage isn’t pretending we’re not frightened, and strength isn’t convincing ourselves that we can handle everything alone.
We can be strong and courageous because God is with us.
And one of the ways we learn to trust Him, particularly when what we see around us gives us reasons to worry, is by continuing to come back to His word.
Prayer # Lord, thank you that you don’t ask us to face life on our own, and that you were with Joshua when he faced something far bigger than he could handle himself.
Help us to be strong and courageous, not because we think we can manage everything ourselves, but because we trust you. Give us a love for your word. Help us not simply to read it, but to think about it, talk about it and allow it to change the way we live.
Help us as a family to encourage one another, be honest with one another, and grow closer to you together.
Amen.

For younger ones # Read together Joshua 1:1–9 NIrV Joshua had a really big job to do, and he might have been scared. But God told him: “Be strong and courageous.”
That didn’t mean Joshua had to be the strongest person or that he was never allowed to feel frightened. God told Joshua why he could be brave: God was going to be with him.
Questions to ask Think about something that sometimes makes you feel scared. Maybe it’s going somewhere new, being in the dark, talking to someone you don’t know, trying something difficult, or doing the right thing when someone else doesn’t want you to.
Can you think of something that you have to be brave to do?
Now imagine doing that thing while holding the hand of someone you really trust. Does it feel a little different when you know you’re not doing it alone? That’s what God wanted Joshua to remember. Joshua had a big job to do, but he didn’t have to do it by himself. And neither do we.
Things to remember Put your hand up and make a big muscle. That’s one kind of strong!
Now put your hand on your heart. There’s another kind of strength: choosing to do what is right even when you’re frightened.
Important message Being brave doesn’t mean I’m never scared. I can be brave because God is with me. Let’s pray God, thank you that you are with me when I’m happy and when I’m scared. Please help me to be brave when something is difficult and help me to remember that I don’t have to face things on my own.
Help me to listen to you and learn more about you.
Amen.

content:
My seven-year-old daughter spends quite a lot of time thinking about the future, usually in the form of questions for me.
“When can I ride a motorbike?” “When can I use that power tool?” “When can I jump off that?”
Sometimes she wants a date. Is it when she’s eight? Ten? A teenager? Sometimes tomorrow seems perfectly reasonable.
What I find fascinating is the ambition behind the questions. She can imagine herself doing almost anything; what she doesn’t yet have is a particularly sophisticated understanding of the risks, dependencies or capabilities involved in getting there. Her horizon is enormous because experience hasn’t yet taught her all the reasons something might be difficult.
Working with organisations, I sometimes see almost the inverse. Experience has taught us a great deal. We know what has failed before, where the controls are, which stakeholders need to be involved and where the organisational or technical complexity lies. All of that experience is valuable, but it can also quietly shape the limits of what we believe is possible.
I’ve started to wonder how often our view of the future is really a reflection of the constraints we’ve accumulated from the past.
Where did the horizon come from? # I was recently looking at a process where an SLA was measured in tens of days. Within that organisation this was normal. It was planned around, measured and perhaps even considered reasonably efficient.
I’ve seen similar activities elsewhere measured in hours.
That doesn’t mean the organisation with the shorter SLA has got it right, or that its answer can simply be transplanted somewhere else. Regulation, risk, technology and the nature of the problem all matter. Comparing organisations without understanding their context isn’t particularly useful.
But knowing that somebody else operates on a radically different timescale changes the question. Instead of asking whether thirty days could become twenty-five, we can ask:
What would have to be true for this to take two hours?
I think one of the privileges of having worked across different industries, organisations and technologies is being able to borrow horizons in this way. You get to see different versions of normal. Something that appears impossibly ambitious in one organisation may be completely routine somewhere else.
I’ve found that useful because it changes the starting point for a conversation. You’re not necessarily importing somebody else’s solution or setting their performance as an arbitrary benchmark. You’re using their experience as evidence that the boundaries of the problem may be wider than the ones immediately visible to you.
Sometimes the most useful thing you can bring into a transformation isn’t an answer. It’s a different reference point.
Organisations carry their history with them # The next question, though, is how our existing horizon came to be where it is.
Most organisational complexity didn’t appear because somebody deliberately set out to make work difficult. Quite often there is a perfectly sensible story behind it. Something went wrong: a release failed, a customer was affected, money was lost or a regulator raised a concern. Perhaps somebody made a decision without the right information or without involving someone who needed to be involved.
We responded to the problem in front of us. We added a review, an approval, another piece of evidence or an additional control. At that moment it may have been entirely the right thing to do. Then something else happened, and we responded again.
Over time, those responses become part of how the organisation works. The people who experienced the original problem move on. Technology changes. Regulation changes. The nature of the risk may change. But the process often remains.
So perhaps nobody ever actually decided that something should take thirty days. Thirty days may simply be the accumulated consequence of a series of individually reasonable decisions made over many years.
I find that distinction important because it changes how we approach transformation. Rather than immediately asking how we reduce thirty days, perhaps we should first understand how thirty days became normal.
Which parts of that timeline manage risks that still exist? Which compensate for a limitation elsewhere? Which exist because of technology we no longer use? Which are genuinely required by regulation, and which have simply become associated with regulation through years of organisational memory?
The current process tells us how the organisation works. It doesn’t necessarily tell us how the organisation needs to work.
Borrow the horizon, not the operating model # There’s an idea here that I think connects with something I took from Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh’s Blitzscaling.
The book deliberately examines an extreme environment: organisations trying to achieve very rapid scale while operating with significant uncertainty. I’m certainly not suggesting that every organisation should attempt to behave like a Silicon Valley hypergrowth company. In many of the environments I work in, doing so would be entirely inappropriate.
What I find useful is the challenge it creates to assumptions about what sensible or responsible management looks like.
Practices that are entirely rational under one set of constraints can become limiting under another. An organisation optimising for rapid growth makes different choices around speed, efficiency and uncertainty from an established organisation operating critical infrastructure. Neither operating model can simply be transplanted into the other.
But looking at the extreme is useful because it changes the reference point. It helps us distinguish between “We can’t do that” and “We have chosen not to do that under our current constraints.” Those are very different statements.
The first closes the conversation. The second invites us to understand the constraints and the choices we’ve made around them. Some will be entirely justified. Others may turn out to be assumptions that have survived longer than the circumstances that created them.
That’s an important part of what I mean by borrowing horizons. Borrow the horizon, not necessarily the operating model.
Risk and frequency # There is something counterintuitive here that I’ve seen repeatedly in technology. When something feels risky, our natural reaction is often to do it less frequently.
Yet one of the most useful lessons I’ve taken from DevOps is almost the opposite: if we want to become good at something, we normally need to do it more often.
That doesn’t mean repeatedly taking the same risk and hoping for a better result. We make the individual change smaller. We automate the things that can be reliably automated. We improve observability, shorten the feedback loop and make it easier to recover when something goes wrong.
The result is that something which used to be an event gradually becomes routine.
I’ve seen releases that once required significant planning, coordination and a room full of people become something teams do many times a day. The underlying need for control hasn’t disappeared. Instead, we’ve changed how that control is achieved and built capability through repetition.
That idea is useful well beyond software delivery. When we do something rarely, knowledge decays between each occurrence and the activity remains exceptional. When we can safely do it more frequently, we create more opportunities to learn, improve and eventually automate parts of it.
This is one reason I think ambition needs more than a bold target. If somebody tells a team accustomed to thirty days that the new target is two hours, it is quite reasonable for them to be sceptical. Their experience tells them something very different.
Borrowing a horizon tells us that a different outcome may be possible. The work of transformation is understanding what needs to change to make that outcome credible.
Looking at the system differently # This is also why I continue to find techniques such as value stream mapping useful. The value isn’t simply in drawing the current process or finding the box with the largest number written beside it. A different horizon gives us a reason to interrogate the system more deeply.
If something takes twelve days, what actually happens during those twelve days? How much of it is work and how much is waiting? Where is judgement genuinely required? Where are we managing risk? Where are we compensating for another constraint in the system? And, perhaps most importantly, which of those things would we design differently if we were starting today?
That last question is becoming increasingly interesting because the capabilities available to us are changing quickly.
AI is an obvious example. There is understandably a lot of interest in identifying activities where AI can improve productivity, but starting with the existing activity can also constrain our thinking.
We might use an LLM to produce in thirty seconds a document that previously took someone three hours to prepare. That’s useful. But if the document then waits four days for somebody to review it, we should probably be curious about the four days as well.
There is also a danger that we assume AI itself must be the answer to each of those questions. It may not be. Sometimes deterministic automation, a policy engine or an existing tool will provide a more predictable answer. In other cases, once we understand why an activity exists, removing it entirely may create more value than automating it.
The important change is that our available capabilities have moved. AI can work with context and information in ways that were difficult to achieve previously. Automation can remove repeatable activity. Modern platforms can make capabilities available on demand that once took weeks to provision. The assumptions that shaped a process five or ten years ago therefore deserve to be revisited.
So the question isn’t simply “Where can we use AI?” or even “What can we automate?”
It’s whether those new capabilities should change what we believe good could look like in the first place.
Making a different future credible # This is where I think borrowing horizons becomes more than benchmarking.
A benchmark tells us how somebody else performs. A horizon helps us imagine a different version of our own organisation.
We can look across industries, at organisations operating at a different scale, at new technologies or simply at teams that have approached the same problem differently. None of those gives us an answer we can copy without thought. What they give us is evidence that the assumptions embedded in our current system aren’t the only assumptions available.
From there, we can work backwards. What prevents that outcome today? Which constraints are fundamental and which have accumulated? What capabilities are missing? Which risks need to be managed differently? Where could shorter feedback loops allow us to learn rather than trying to design the entire future upfront?
That feels more useful to me than simply telling organisations to be more ambitious. Ambition without an understanding of risk is easy. The more interesting leadership challenge is retaining the ability to imagine something radically different after you’ve learned how complicated the world really is.
Perhaps that’s something I want my daughter to retain too.
As she gets older, she’ll inevitably develop a better understanding of why she can’t do everything tomorrow. That’s a good thing. But I hope that understanding risk doesn’t stop her looking at something new and asking, “When can I do that?”
Organisations could probably afford to ask that question a little more often too. Not because somebody else doing something means we should simply copy them, but because their experience gives us another horizon against which to test our own assumptions.
If that is possible somewhere else, what would have to be true for it to become normal here?

content:
Most AI coding setups still look suspiciously like a faster version of the way we have always developed software. A developer asks for a change, an AI model explores some files, writes some code, perhaps runs a few tests, and returns the result. Add more specialised agents and the flow becomes more sophisticated — an architect creates a plan, an explorer inspects the repository, a developer implements the change and a reviewer checks the result — but fundamentally it is still a pipeline.
I think the more interesting shift is to stop treating AI-assisted development as a sequence of activities and instead design it as a closed engineering loop. The distinction matters. Rather than asking an agent to implement a change, ask the engineering system to reach a desired state and produce enough evidence that it has done so. Once you take that seriously, the architecture changes quite quickly, because the system needs more than tools and context. It needs persistent engineering memory.
As I have been working through this locally, that has also changed how I think about the role of the knowledge graph. I still think the graph is important, but it is not the whole answer. What we really need is a persistent model that joins intent, architecture, source code, evidence, history and semantic context, and allows agents to interrogate that model in different ways depending on the problem they are trying to solve.
From pipeline to engineering loop # My current local coding environment already uses a set of specialist roles around OpenCode: Architect, Explorer, Developer, Reviewer and Documenter. The obvious first architecture looks like this:
flowchart LR A[Intent] --> B[Architect] B --> C[Explorer] C --> D[Developer] D --> E[Reviewer] E --> F[Documenter]There is nothing particularly wrong with that model, but it has an obvious limitation: the process has an end. If the reviewer identifies a problem, we generally rely on another prompt or another human action to restart the process. That feels like the wrong abstraction. A stronger model is a feedback loop.
flowchart TD A[Intent / Requirement] --> B[Architect] B --> C[Explorer] C --> D[Developer] D --> E[Deterministic Verification] D --> F[Semantic Review] E --> G[Evidence] F --> G G --> H{Desired state evidenced?} H -- No --> I[Reason about gap] I --> C H -- Yes --> J[Document / Curate] J --> K[Engineering Memory] K --> BThe core cycle becomes Intent → change → observe → compare → reason → change. That is not a new idea in engineering. It is the same feedback principle that underpins DevOps, continuous delivery and most mature engineering systems. The difference is that we are now making that loop explicit for AI and giving the agents enough persistent context to reason across iterations rather than rebuilding their understanding every time.
Engineering against a desired state # Consider a simple request: “Add authentication.” A conventional coding agent may interpret that primarily as an implementation task, but a loop-oriented engineering system should first turn it into a desired state.
Capability: Authenticated access Constraints: OAuth/OIDC Microsoft Entra No credentials stored locally Acceptance: Unauthenticated requests are rejected User identity is propagated downstream Role policies are enforced Automated tests demonstrate all three That changes the nature of the work. The developer is no longer simply trying to generate plausible authentication code; the engineering loop is trying to make the observed state of the software satisfy these conditions. After implementation, the useful output may look more like this:
Build PASS Unit tests PASS Integration tests FAIL Security checks PASS Architecture checks PASS The failed integration test is not simply an error message. It is evidence that the desired state has not yet been reached, and that evidence should drive the next iteration.
The missing piece is persistent understanding # Once you model development this way, another problem becomes obvious: how does each agent understand the software system? Today, most coding agents repeatedly reconstruct context from source files, README files, architecture notes, Git history, search results, the current prompt and whatever still fits inside the context window. This works surprisingly well, but much of the system model remains implicit and every agent is rebuilding some version of the same understanding.
My first instinct was to solve that with a knowledge graph. I still think that is part of the answer, but only part. A graph is extremely good at answering questions such as “what implements this requirement?”, “which tests verify this capability?” or “what components depend on this service?”, but not every form of engineering memory is naturally graph-shaped.
Test runs, build history, execution times, commits and observations are often relational. Documentation and source fragments benefit from semantic similarity. Architecture decisions need both structured identity and rich textual context. Git remains uniquely good at recording authored change over time. The better architecture is therefore not simply a graph for coding agents, but an engineering memory system with several complementary ways of understanding the same estate.
The graph still matters # A basic code graph might tell us:
AuthController CALLS AuthService Useful, but relatively low-level. What I want the engineering graph to represent is the chain between business intent and observable engineering evidence.
flowchart TD R[Requirement] C[Capability] S[Service / Component] CODE[Code] ADR[Architecture Decision] T[Test] E[Evidence] R -->|SATISFIED_BY| C C -->|REALISED_BY| S S -->|IMPLEMENTED_BY| CODE S -->|CONSTRAINED_BY| ADR R -->|VERIFIED_BY| T T -->|PRODUCES| EOther relationships can sit alongside these:
Component DEPENDS_ON Component API EXPOSES Capability Change MODIFIES Component Incident CAUSED_BY Component Test VERIFIES Requirement ADR CONSTRAINS Component Now an agent is no longer just navigating files. It can reason about the relationship between intent, implementation and evidence. That is where the graph earns its place, but it should be one view of engineering memory rather than the entire storage model.
From graph database to multi-model engineering memory # My initial design was to keep an authored representation in Git, load it into a graph database, and let the agents interrogate that runtime graph.
flowchart LR GIT[Git] --> JSON[Graph files] JSON --> GRAPH[(Graph Database)] GRAPH --> AGENTS[Agents]It is elegant, but it starts to look too narrow once you consider what the system actually needs to remember. There are several different classes of engineering knowledge.
flowchart TD A[Intentional Knowledge] B[Structural Knowledge] C[Historical Evidence] D[Semantic Context] A --> M[Engineering Memory] B --> M C --> M D --> MIntentional knowledge includes requirements, capabilities, architecture decisions and explicit constraints. Structural knowledge includes imports, calls, dependencies, APIs, schemas and relationships discovered from code. Historical evidence includes builds, tests, deployments, failures, observations and changes over time. Semantic context includes documents, code chunks, incidents and concepts that may be related even where no explicit relationship has yet been established.
Trying to force all of that into one graph representation is possible. I am no longer convinced it is desirable.
PostgreSQL as the engineering memory foundation # The architecture I am now leaning towards uses PostgreSQL as the foundation, with different models layered over it.
flowchart TD G[Git / Authored Intent] S[Source Code] R[Runtime & CI Evidence] I[Engineering Memory Ingestion] PG[(PostgreSQL)] REL[Relational State] AGE[Apache AGEGraph] VEC[pgvectorSemantic Similarity] FTS[Full Text Search] CTX[Context Builder] A[OpenCode Agents] G --> I S --> I R --> I I --> PG PG --> REL PG --> AGE PG --> VEC PG --> FTS REL --> CTX AGE --> CTX VEC --> CTX FTS --> CTX CTX --> AThis feels like a better fit because each mechanism can be used where it is strongest. Normal PostgreSQL tables handle structured engineering state and evidence. Apache AGE provides graph traversal over explicit relationships. pgvector provides fuzzy semantic retrieval. PostgreSQL full-text search handles lexical discovery. Git remains the durable record of authored intent and source history.
The important bit is that the agents do not need to care which mechanism answered the question. They need a useful, bounded context.
Different questions need different retrieval models # This becomes obvious when you look at the types of questions an engineering agent actually asks. Graph traversal is ideal for questions such as “what implements this requirement?”, “what depends on this component?”, “which ADR constrains this service?” or “which tests verify this capability?”. Relational queries are better for “which tests failed after this commit?”, “what was the duration of the last ten builds?”, “when was this component last changed?” or “which evidence was collected for this requirement?”.
Semantic retrieval helps with a different class of question again: “have we seen a similar failure before?”, “which architecture decisions appear relevant to this problem?” or “what other parts of the estate discuss the same business concept?”. And ordinary text search remains extremely useful for finding an ADR by number, locating references to a service, or finding the configuration containing an endpoint.
The interesting capability is not choosing one retrieval model. It is composing them.
The context builder becomes the important boundary # That changes one part of the architecture quite significantly. Earlier, I imagined a small graphctl utility sitting in front of the graph database. I still like the idea of a stable interface, but its responsibility is now broader than graph access. Call it graphctl, engmem, or something else; the name matters less than the abstraction.
An agent might ask:
explain test:T92 The engineering-memory layer could then perform several operations:
flowchart TD Q[Explain Test T92] SQL[SQLLatest failure & history] G[AGERequirement & component relationships] V[pgvectorSimilar failures / ADRs] H[GitRecent changes] C[Bounded Context] Q --> SQL Q --> G Q --> V Q --> H SQL --> C G --> C V --> C H --> CThe resulting context might say that T92 verifies R127, R127 is satisfied by capability C14, C14 is primarily implemented by S7 and S9, S7 changed in the current commit, the test was passing before that change, a previous incident involving missing identity claims affected the same component, and ADR-017 defines the expected identity mechanism.
That is a very different starting point from “here is the repository, a test failed, work it out.” The value of the memory layer is that it turns a large search problem into a bounded reasoning problem.
The Architect manages desired state # This also changes the role of the Architect agent. Rather than producing an implementation plan and disappearing, the Architect can define the desired engineering state. Imagine asking: “Add Xero integration.”
The existing model may describe:
Financial Reporting ├── Bank data ├── Donations └── Budgeting The desired state may introduce:
Financial Reporting ├── Bank data ├── Donations ├── Budgeting └── Xero Integration ├── OAuth lifecycle ├── Tenant mapping ├── Account mapping ├── Transaction import └── Reconciliation rules The work becomes a transformation:
flowchart LR A[Current State] B[Desired State] C[Delta] D[Implementation] E[Observed Evidence] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> EThe important part is that the desired state is persistent. The developer, verifier and reviewer are all working against the same model rather than a series of loosely connected prompts.
Explorer becomes a curator of understanding # Explorer then becomes responsible for keeping engineering memory aligned with reality. Some relationships can be discovered deterministically: imports, function calls, package dependencies, API routes, database schemas, infrastructure resources, tests and pipelines. Others require inference.
For example:
TrusteeService IMPLEMENTS Trustee Eligibility That may not be directly represented anywhere in the source. An LLM may infer it from names, behaviour, documentation and surrounding context. That distinction matters, so every assertion should carry some notion of source and provenance.
{ "from": "svc:trustee-service", "type": "IMPLEMENTS", "to": "cap:trustee-eligibility", "source": "explorer", "provenance": "src/services/TrusteeService.ts", "confidence": 0.91 } A relationship derived from an AST, a relationship explicitly authored by an architect, and a relationship inferred by a model should not silently carry the same authority. Engineering memory needs to know not just what it believes, but why it believes it.
pgvector is not just there for RAG # This is one of the parts I find particularly interesting. It is easy to think about vector search purely as a mechanism for feeding documents into an LLM, but in this architecture its role is broader.
The graph describes relationships we have explicitly established:
AuthService IMPLEMENTS Authentication Vector similarity helps us discover relationships that may exist:
Identity federation ADR Missing claims incident SSO requirement Authentication implementation That gives us a useful flow:
flowchart LR V[Semantic Similarity] I[Agent Inference] A[Candidate Assertion] E[Evidence] G[Established Graph Relationship] V --> I I --> A A --> E E --> GThe probabilistic mechanisms help us discover possibilities. Evidence and deliberate engineering decisions determine which of those possibilities deserve to become durable relationships. That pattern mirrors the broader principle behind the entire architecture.
Git remains important, but it does not contain everything # I still think Git should contain the things the engineering team deliberately asserts: requirements, ADRs, architecture definitions and perhaps explicit semantic relationships.
engineering/ ├── requirements/ ├── capabilities/ ├── adr/ ├── architecture/ └── relationships/ What I would no longer do is try to serialise the entire operational graph back into Git. There will eventually be far too much derived state: function relationships, embeddings, historical test results, build evidence, observations, confidence scores and agent discoveries. Persisting all of that as source-controlled JSON would create noise and duplicate information that can be derived again.
Git therefore remains an authoritative source, but not the only source.
flowchart TD G[GitIntent & Source History] P[(PostgreSQLOperational Engineering Memory)] R[RuntimeObserved Reality] L[LLMWorking Memory] G --> P R --> P P --> L L --> PThe distinction is useful: LLM context is working memory. PostgreSQL is operational engineering memory. Git is authored and historical record. Runtime and verification provide observed reality. None of those should be confused with the others.
Do not rebuild the memory every time # This also changes the startup model. When I was treating the graph database as a projection of Git, rebuilding it on startup seemed reasonable. With engineering memory, that no longer makes sense because historical observations are part of the value.
We want to be able to ask when a dependency first appeared, whether a failure has happened before, whether a test is historically flaky, what the architecture looked like when a decision was made, or which commit introduced a particular behaviour. The database should therefore persist across sessions and accumulate useful engineering context over time.
Startup becomes incremental:
flowchart TD A[Start Environment] B[Start PostgreSQL] C[Check Extensions / Migrations] D[Compare Indexed Commit to HEAD] E[Analyse Changed Files] F[Update Relationships] G[Refresh Embeddings Where Required] H[OpenCode Ready] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G G --> HThat is much closer to the mental model of an experienced engineer joining a long-running product than an agent waking up with amnesia every time a new conversation starts.
Debugging becomes graph-guided, evidence-backed and semantically assisted # Consider again a failing test. Without engineering memory, the agent gets:
Test T92 failed. and now has to search.
With engineering memory:
flowchart TD T[Test T92] R[Requirement R127] C[Capability C14] S[Service S7] CH[Recent Commit] ADR[ADR-017] INC[Similar Previous Incident] T -->|VERIFIES| R R -->|SATISFIED_BY| C C -->|IMPLEMENTED_BY| S CH -->|MODIFIED| S S -->|CONSTRAINED_BY| ADR INC -. semantically related .-> TNow the agent can begin with the knowledge that T92 verifies requirement R127, R127 is implemented primarily by S7 and S9, S7 changed in the latest commit, ADR-017 constrains its identity behaviour, and a previous incident involving missing claims has strong semantic similarity to this failure.
That is not simply better retrieval. It is a fundamentally better reasoning environment.
The agents become responsibilities rather than separate models # At this point I would describe the system in terms of six responsibilities, not necessarily six separately running models.
Architect — intent: defines requirements, constraints, architecture decisions and desired state.
Explorer — understanding: continuously hydrates and challenges engineering memory against the actual software.
Developer — action: changes software, infrastructure and configuration.
Verifier — observation: executes deterministic tests, builds, scans and checks.
Reviewer — judgement: asks whether the collected evidence demonstrates the intended outcome without violating architectural constraints.
Documenter / Curator — memory: turns useful learning into durable engineering context.
Around those sits an orchestrator:
while desired_state != evidenced_state: determine_next_action() execute() collect_evidence() update_engineering_memory() evaluate_difference() That loop obviously needs boundaries: iteration limits, cost controls, permissions, escalation points and clear rules about which actions an agent is allowed to perform autonomously. The point is not to build an infinitely autonomous developer. The point is to build a controlled engineering system that can continue working towards a desired state, while making its evidence and decisions visible.
Start smaller than the architecture diagram suggests # It would be easy to turn this into a platform project before proving that the loop itself is useful. I would start with PostgreSQL, a small relational schema for requirements and evidence, Apache AGE for a limited set of explicit relationships, pgvector for semantic retrieval, and a thin context-building interface for the agents. The first implementation only needs to connect one requirement to the components that realise it, the tests that verify it and the evidence produced by a run.
Then prove one loop.
flowchart TD A[Architect defines desired state] B[Engineering memory records intent] C[Developer changes source] D[Explorer updates understanding] E[Verifier runs checks] F[Evidence enters memory] G[Reviewer evaluates state] H{Satisfied?} A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G G --> H H -- No --> C H -- Yes --> I[Document and curate]Only after that loop works would I expand the ontology, automate more ingestion, add richer semantic discovery or introduce more elaborate orchestration. The database architecture matters, but the value is in the behaviour it enables.
The bigger idea # What I find interesting is that this is converging on the same architecture I keep arriving at when thinking about enterprise AI. In the enterprise context: ontology + context + deterministic systems + AI reasoning + agents + memory. In a software engineering environment: engineering memory + deterministic tools + AI reasoning + specialist responsibilities + observed evidence. They are expressions of the same principle.
AI should not own truth. It should reason over a structured representation of truth, act through controlled mechanisms, observe the result, and continuously reconcile its model with reality.
That may turn out to matter more than simply giving coding agents larger models or larger context windows. The interesting evolution is not just from coding assistant to coding agent. It is from coding agent to engineering system.
summary: Most AI coding setups still look suspiciously like a faster version of the way we have always developed software. A developer asks for a change, an AI model explores some files, writes some code, perhaps runs a few tests, and returns the result. Add more specialised agents and the flow becomes more sophisticated — an architect creates a plan, an explorer inspects the repository, a developer implements the change and a reviewer checks the result — but fundamentally it is still a pipeline.
title: From Coding Agents to Loop Engineering: Building Engineering Memory for AI
