After hours · a continuing series Late Night Questions My wife is a midwife, and some of the more difficult theological and ethical questions in our house have a habit of arriving after a late shift, usually when we're both tired and neither of us is expecting a theological discussion.
This series is an attempt to keep track of those questions: not necessarily to find a neat answer, but to look at Scripture, draw on writers who have helped me think, and work out what I actually believe and why.
Tonight's questionIf God already knows, why pray?
Key passages: Scripture Daniel 9:1–3 NIV and Scripture Matthew 6:5–13 NIV Tap or hover over either reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
The particular version of the question was slightly more difficult than that. We were talking about praying for people to come to know Jesus. Scripture tells us that God is patient, “not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). If that’s God’s desire, why do I need to ask him for it? Am I trying to convince God to do something he already wants to do? If God knows the person, knows their heart and knows the outcome, what exactly is my prayer adding?
Daniel does something strange # Daniel 9 gives us an interesting place to start because Daniel seems to face a version of exactly this problem. At the beginning of the chapter, Daniel has been reading Jeremiah. He understands from Jeremiah’s prophecy that the desolation of Jerusalem is to last seventy years (Daniel 9:2; Jeremiah 25:11–12; 29:10). Daniel isn’t praying because he is trying to discover what God intends to do. God has already spoken about what he intends to do.
The obvious response might be to put the scroll down and wait. If God is sovereign, and God has said that after seventy years he will restore his people, what possible difference can Daniel make? Except Daniel does almost the exact opposite:
“So I turned to the Lord God and pleaded with him in prayer and petition…”
— Daniel 9:3
It’s the “so” that catches my attention. Daniel understands the promise, so he prays. Knowing what God intends to do doesn’t make prayer unnecessary; it becomes the reason for Daniel’s prayer. That begins to challenge one of my assumptions about what prayer is for. If prayer is primarily about informing God of a problem or persuading him towards a particular course of action, Daniel’s behaviour doesn’t make much sense. But perhaps that’s because I’ve started with the wrong model of prayer.
God knows. Ask anyway. # Jesus makes the apparent contradiction even more explicit in Matthew 6. Before teaching the disciples how to pray, he tells them:
“Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.”
— Matthew 6:8
Then, almost immediately, he teaches them to ask. Give us our daily bread. Forgive us. Lead us. Deliver us. And, perhaps most relevant to the question we’re asking:
“Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.”
— Matthew 6:10
Jesus tells us in the same passage that God knows what we need before we ask and that we should ask him anyway. More than that, part of the model prayer Jesus gives us is explicitly asking for God’s will to be done. That suggests prayer can’t simply be the transfer of information from us to God. I’m not telling an omniscient God something he has somehow missed. Nor does prayer make much sense as an attempt to wear down a reluctant God until he eventually agrees with me. Jesus describes the person we’re addressing not as a distant decision-maker who needs lobbying, but as “your Father.”
C. S. Lewis wrestled with this problem too. Across his writing on prayer he returns to the strange relationship between petition and providence: if God knows and God acts, in what sense can our requests really matter? Lewis doesn’t reduce prayer to a technique where the right amount of faith, or the right combination of words, produces the desired result. He is willing to leave some of the tension intact. I find that helpful because Scripture seems quite comfortable doing the same.
Prayer as participation # I wonder whether Daniel gives us at least part of the answer. Prayer isn’t simply asking God to change his plans; it is one of the ways he allows us to participate in them. There is a pattern here that extends beyond prayer. God could proclaim the gospel without us, but sends people to proclaim it. He cares for the poor, but repeatedly tells his people to care for them. He provides for people, while inviting us to be generous. God’s ability to accomplish something without us doesn’t appear to be an argument, in Scripture, for us doing nothing.
Perhaps prayer belongs in that same pattern. When I pray for someone to come to know Jesus, I’m not trying to persuade God to start caring about them. I’m bringing someone I care about before a Father who already cares about them more perfectly than I do. I’m asking him to act, but I’m also aligning myself with something I already know to be close to his heart.
Paul seems quite comfortable holding those ideas together. In Romans 10:1 he writes:
“My heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is that they may be saved.”
There is no sense that God’s desire for salvation makes Paul’s intercession pointless. It appears to do the opposite. Daniel takes that participation even further. His prayer isn’t “they have sinned”; it is “we have sinned.” He identifies himself with his people, confesses with them and asks God for mercy. Prayer doesn’t leave Daniel as a spectator waiting for God to fulfil a prophecy. It draws him into what God is doing.
Prayer changes things # There is a temptation at this point to tidy the problem up by saying that prayer doesn’t change our circumstances; prayer changes us. There is clearly truth in the second half of that. Daniel’s prayer changes his posture towards his people, and spending time praying for someone will almost inevitably affect the way I think about and behave towards them. But I don’t think Scripture allows me to accept the first half.
Prayer changes things.
James tells us that “the prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective” (James 5:16). Abraham intercedes. Moses intercedes. Paul repeatedly asks churches to pray for him. The early church prays for Peter when he is imprisoned and, rather dramatically, Peter turns up at the door while they are still praying (Acts 12). These people don’t behave as though prayer is simply a reflective exercise designed to alter their own state of mind. They expect God to act.
Healing makes this even harder to turn into something purely metaphorical or psychological. Jesus heals throughout the Gospels. He doesn’t merely speak about the possibility of healing; it is a substantial part of his ministry, and he commissions his disciples to heal too (Matthew 10:1, 7–8). The pattern continues through Acts, and James tells a sick person to call the elders of the church specifically so that they can pray for them (James 5:14–16).
For me, then, the question isn’t really whether God heals or whether prayer can change circumstances. God heals. God intervenes. Prayer matters. I have enough reason in Scripture to believe that, and enough stories from people I know personally that I am not willing to explain it away. I have a friend who was given around six months to live more than twenty years ago. He is still here. Personal testimony alone doesn’t form the foundation for Christian doctrine, and I don’t pretend to know the medical or spiritual mechanics behind every story, but testimony matters. In one sense the gospel itself is testimony — good news about what God has done — and the witness of those who saw the risen Jesus sits at the heart of the New Testament. Experiences like this don’t establish doctrine by themselves, but they sit comfortably alongside what I already find in Scripture: God still acts.
That doesn’t make the subject easier. In some ways it makes it considerably harder, because I also know people who haven’t been healed. Our own family has lived with chronic illness for years. We have prayed, other people have prayed, and we continue to believe that God heals while living with the reality that the healing we would dearly love to see has not happened.
But I don’t think the answer to that tension is to weaken the first statement until the tension disappears. Nor is it to blame someone who remains ill for somehow failing to generate enough faith. God heals. We should pray for healing. And sometimes, having prayed, we are still waiting. Why that is deserves its own question rather than an easy answer here.
Exactly how God’s action in response to prayer fits alongside his sovereignty and foreknowledge is also something Christians have debated for a very long time. I don’t expect to resolve that in a late-night conversation with my wife or in a blog post. But I don’t need to understand all of the mechanics before I pray. Daniel certainly doesn’t. He knows what God has said, he trusts God’s character, and because of those things he asks God to act.
There may be more happening than we can see # There is another picture of prayer that has stayed with me for years, although it comes from fiction rather than theology. I love Frank Peretti’s novels, particularly the way he depicts ordinary Christians praying while, unseen by them, a spiritual battle is taking place around the events they are praying about. Someone is simply praying in a room, apparently doing very little, while Peretti allows the reader to see a completely different perspective on what that prayer might mean.
I’d be careful about taking that picture too literally. This Present Darkness and Piercing the Darkness are novels, not field guides to the spiritual realm. Conversations about spiritual warfare can quite quickly move from what Scripture actually tells us into elaborate systems built on speculation. Perhaps partly because of that risk, spiritual warfare isn’t a particularly popular subject in many of the church conversations I’ve been part of. But avoiding speculation shouldn’t mean avoiding the subject altogether.
Scripture is quite clear that there is a spiritual reality beyond what we see. Paul tells the Ephesian church that:
“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood…”
— Ephesians 6:12
He goes on to describe rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil. Then, having described the armour of God, he tells them to “pray in the Spirit on all occasions” (Ephesians 6:18). And strangely enough, Daniel gives us perhaps one of the clearest glimpses of this too.
In Daniel 10, he has been mourning and praying for three weeks when a messenger finally arrives. Daniel is told that his words were heard from the first day, but that the messenger had been opposed by the “prince of the Persian kingdom” until Michael came to help (Daniel 10:12–13). There is a lot there that I don’t pretend to understand, and perhaps that is important: Scripture gives us a glimpse, not a diagram.
I’m wary of pretending that I know exactly what is happening in the spiritual realm when someone prays. Scripture doesn’t give us enough information to construct the mechanics, and Peretti’s imaginative picture shouldn’t become our theology. But Daniel 10 does make it difficult to describe prayer as merely a psychological exercise which helps me feel differently about my circumstances. Daniel is praying in the world he can see while something he cannot see is happening at the same time.
Perhaps Peretti’s fictional picture has stayed with me because it gives an imaginative form to that mystery. I don’t know what happens in the spiritual realm when we pray, but Scripture gives me reason to believe that prayer matters beyond simply changing me. As the popular worship song puts it: when I fight, I fight on my knees. Perhaps there is more truth in that picture than we sometimes allow ourselves to talk about.
Prayer as a way of living # There’s a line attributed to Smith Wigglesworth that I’ve always loved. In one form, it goes something like:
“I don’t often spend more than half an hour in prayer at one time, but I never go more than half an hour without praying.”
There are plenty of stories about Wigglesworth, and some aspects of his ministry and particularly his approach to healing deserve a much longer conversation. But this description of prayer has always resonated with me. It describes prayer less as an event and more as a posture.
Prayer doesn’t have to mean finding thirty uninterrupted minutes, adopting the right position and working through a list. It can be the continuing conversation that runs through the day: asking, thanking, questioning, listening, interceding, sometimes simply saying help. Paul’s instruction to “pray continually” (1 Thessalonians 5:17) begins to make much more sense viewed this way. It isn’t necessarily an instruction to spend every waking moment in formal prayer. It is an invitation to a life in which the conversation with God is never particularly far away.
And perhaps this changes the original question. If prayer is simply a mechanism for submitting requests, then God’s foreknowledge creates a genuine efficiency problem. Why submit information he already has? Why ask for something he already intends to do? But if prayer is relationship, participation and — somehow — part of a spiritual reality larger than the one I can see, then perhaps efficiency was never the point.
Perhaps I’ve been asking the wrong question # I think part of my problem is that I’ve approached prayer as though it were primarily a mechanism. If God already has the information and already knows the outcome, what function does my request perform? Jesus starts somewhere else: “Our Father…”
My children regularly tell me things I already know. They ask me for things I already know they need. Sometimes they ask for things I’ve already decided to give them. The conversation isn’t made redundant by my prior knowledge, because transferring information isn’t the only reason we’re talking. There is a relationship between us. That analogy only takes us so far, of course. I’m not omniscient, and my relationship with my children doesn’t solve the theological problem of divine sovereignty and human agency. But it does make me wonder whether I’ve been trying to answer a relational question in purely mechanical terms.
Daniel discovers what God has promised, and so he prays. Jesus tells us our Father already knows what we need, and so he teaches us to ask. Daniel prays in one realm while Scripture gives us a glimpse of a conflict happening in another. And throughout Scripture people pray expecting that God will actually act.
Maybe prayer isn’t about giving God information at all. Perhaps it is about relationship with our Father, participation in what he is doing and engagement with a reality of which we currently see only a very small part. We’re not trying to persuade God to become good. We’re not reminding him of something he’s forgotten. We’re asking him to act, aligning ourselves with what he is doing and accepting his invitation to participate in it.
That doesn’t answer every question about prayer. In fact, it creates several more, and some of those are considerably harder. If God heals, why doesn’t he always heal? What do we do when we’ve prayed for the same thing for years? If God can bring good out of suffering, does that mean the suffering itself was somehow good? What does it actually mean to pray “your will be done” when his will isn’t what we desperately want?
Those are probably questions for another late night.
References and further reading # Daniel 9–10 — particularly Daniel 9:2–3 and 10:12–13. Read together, these chapters give a fascinating picture of Daniel understanding God’s purposes, responding in prayer, and then being given a glimpse of a spiritual reality beyond what he could see.
Matthew 6:5–13 — Jesus’ teaching on prayer. Particularly the tension between “your Father knows what you need before you ask him” and Jesus immediately teaching his disciples to ask.
Matthew 10:1, 7–8; Acts 3; Acts 9; James 5:14–18 — examples of healing, intercession and the expectation that God acts in response to prayer in the ministry of Jesus, the apostles and the life of the church.
Ephesians 6:10–20 — Paul’s description of spiritual conflict, the armour of God and prayer.
C. S. Lewis, writing on prayer — Lewis wrestles in several places with petitionary prayer, providence and the difficult question of how our requests can matter to an omniscient and sovereign God. Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer is particularly relevant.
Frank E. Peretti, This Present Darkness and Piercing the Darkness — fiction rather than theology, but an imaginative depiction of prayer occurring alongside an unseen spiritual conflict. Useful as a picture, rather than a description of how the spiritual realm necessarily operates.
Smith Wigglesworth — particularly the saying attributed to him about rarely praying for more than thirty minutes while rarely going thirty minutes without praying, which captures prayer as an ongoing way of life rather than simply a scheduled activity.

Read: Scripture Joshua 1:1–9 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 27 NIV There are many things that can make us afraid. Sometimes we know exactly what we are frightened of; sometimes we simply feel afraid and cannot explain why. Our thoughts can become confused, things that once seemed familiar can feel uncertain, and we may wonder what is happening or what will happen next.
But there is something that has not changed: God is with you. He has not moved away from you, he has not forgotten you, and he has not stopped loving you. Again and again in the Bible, God tells his people, “Do not be afraid.” He does not say this because there is never anything frightening in life, but because we do not face those things alone.
Joshua — God was not finished with him # Joshua knew what it was to wait. He had already spent decades serving alongside Moses, watching God lead Israel and learning to trust him. Then Moses died and Joshua found himself facing a new chapter. He was not being asked simply to look back on everything God had already done; God still had work for him to do.
At precisely the moment when Joshua might have felt the weight of the past and uncertainty about the future, God said:
Scripture Joshua 1:9 NIV Joshua’s courage did not come from pretending that nothing frightening lay ahead. It came from remembering who was with him. The God who had been faithful through the wilderness had not changed, and God was not finished with Joshua yet.
That same God is your God. Because you belong to Jesus, God has made his home with you. The Bible says:
Scripture 1 John 4:4 NIV Fear can feel very big. A troubling thought can feel very big. Something we cannot understand can feel very big. But Jesus is greater. You do not have to win every argument in your mind or understand everything that is happening. You can come back to one simple truth: Jesus is with me. Jesus loves me. I belong to Jesus. I do not need to be afraid.
Read Psalm 27 # Psalm 27 gives us words to use when fear feels close. It begins with a question worth holding onto: “The Lord is my light and my salvation—whom shall I fear?” The psalm does not pretend that there are no enemies, troubles or frightening circumstances. Instead, David keeps returning his attention to God: his light, his salvation and his stronghold.
Read the whole psalm slowly. You do not need to remember every line. Notice the repeated confidence that God is present and trustworthy, and finish with its invitation to wait for the Lord and take heart.
Remember # Your feelings can change, your circumstances can change, and even some of the things you remember may become difficult to hold onto. But God does not change. Like Joshua, you can look back on years in which God has been faithful and still look forward believing that he has not finished with you.
Jesus said:
Scripture John 10:28 NIV You are held by him. Your security does not depend upon how strongly you can hold onto God; he is holding onto you. You are still here, still loved, still held, and God is still at work in your life.
Say this together # I belong to Jesus. God is with me. God has not forgotten me. Greater is he who is in me. God is not finished with me. I do not need to be afraid.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you are with me. When I feel afraid, help me remember that I belong to you. Thank you for the example of Joshua and for the reminder that you were still leading him into new things after many years of walking with you.
Thank you that Jesus is greater than anything that frightens me, that you have not forgotten me, and that nothing can take me out of your hand. Help me to remember your faithfulness, trust you for what is ahead, and know that you are still at work in me. Give me your peace today.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

content:
There are some things we know are important and yet still struggle to do consistently.
Reading the Bible has, at different points in my life, been one of those things. Family devotions have been another. I have ADHD, and consistency and discipline are things I’ve always struggled with. I can become deeply absorbed in something, build a routine around it and then, somehow, find that routine has disappeared. There have been periods when I’ve read Scripture regularly and periods when I’ve let it drift. In recent years the same has happened with sitting down regularly as a family to read the Bible and pray together.
That’s something I want to change.
A responsibility I don’t want to ignore # As a dad, I believe I have a responsibility for how I raise my children. I want my girls to grow up loving the Lord, knowing His word and learning what it means to live a life that honours Him. Of course, I can’t manufacture faith in them. Their relationship with God has to become their own. But Scripture doesn’t therefore leave me as a passive observer of that journey.
Psalm 78 describes one generation telling the next “the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done” so that the next generation would know them and, ultimately, “put their trust in God” (Psalm 78:4–7). Proverbs carries the same idea through the picture of parents actively forming and instructing their children. Proverbs 4 begins, “Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction,” before the writer remembers being taught by his own father (Proverbs 4:1–4). There is something deliberately generational about faith and wisdom being taught, modelled and passed on.
The New Testament even treats what happens within someone’s family as relevant evidence of their readiness to lead elsewhere. When Paul describes the qualifications for an overseer, he says that they should manage their own family well, asking: “If anyone does not know how to manage his own family, how can he take care of God’s church?” (1 Timothy 3:4–5; see also Titus 1:6). That passage is specifically about church leadership, so I don’t want to stretch it into something it isn’t. But the principle challenges me: leadership and discipleship don’t begin when I walk through the doors of a church. My character and faithfulness at home matter.
So I can talk about God with my girls, pray with them, answer their questions and, perhaps most importantly, keep bringing us back to Scripture together. Proverbs 22:6 captures something of that responsibility: “Start children off on the way they should go…” It isn’t a formula guaranteeing how our children will eventually respond — their faith must become their own — but it does remind me that the direction in which I help them start matters.
That makes my own inconsistency matter beyond me. Scripture talks about the renewing of our minds. Joshua is told to meditate on God’s word day and night. Psalm 1 describes the person who delights in God’s instruction and meditates on it day and night as being like a tree planted beside streams of water. Again and again, we’re presented with God’s word not merely as information to learn but as something that shapes us.
If I believe that, I need to make room for it.
Not another perfect plan # My natural response to recognising a problem like this can be to design a system. I could map out the next year, build a reading programme, create a schedule and decide exactly what we’re going to cover each week. I’m deliberately not doing that.
Instead, I’m borrowing an idea from another part of my life and taking something closer to an agile, just-in-time approach. I’ll normally write these devotions the day before we use them, perhaps sometimes that morning. We’ll work through one together, see where the conversation goes, and allow that to influence what we explore next. That also means these aren’t being written retrospectively after I’ve worked everything out. They’re part of my attempt to become more consistent myself.
In that sense, starting again is part of the lesson. Consistency doesn’t have to mean never missing a day or never getting something wrong. Sometimes faithfulness means noticing that something important has drifted and choosing to begin again.
Learning together # There’s another challenge I want to embrace. Our three girls are at very different stages. Something that engages a thirteen-year-old isn’t necessarily going to make sense to a seven-year-old, while something aimed entirely at a seven-year-old isn’t likely to produce much discussion with an eleven- and thirteen-year-old.
So these aren’t intended to be lectures. Each devotion will start with a passage of Scripture and a few ideas and questions we can explore together. I’ll write the main discussion at a level that gives the older girls — and Louise and me — something meaningful to wrestle with. Where it helps, I’ll include a simpler section for younger children that gets to the heart of the same idea through shorter questions, examples and activities.
I don’t expect to have all the answers either. There will be things Louise and I can teach our girls. There will be things they notice that we’ve missed. There will be questions we can answer, others we’ll need to investigate, and probably some where we’ll simply have to say, “I don’t know.”
That’s okay.
The aim isn’t to become a family who knows all the answers. The aim is to become a family who knows God better.
Beginning with courage # We’re going to start in Joshua 1. It’s a passage I remember connecting with when I was younger: “Be strong and courageous.” But there’s much more in those words than a motivational slogan. Joshua is facing uncertainty and responsibility. God tells him repeatedly to be courageous, reminds Joshua that He is with him, and tells him to keep returning to His word.
That seems an appropriate place for us to begin. And perhaps starting this series requires a little courage from me too — not because writing a devotion is particularly frightening, but because putting this into practice means acknowledging where I’ve been inconsistent and deciding that I don’t want that inconsistency to have the final word.
So we’re starting again. Not with a year’s worth of material or a perfect plan. Just with Joshua 1, a Bible around the table, and a family learning together.
The first family devotion is now available: Be Strong and Courageous, exploring Joshua 1 and what courage looks like when we understand that God is with us.

Read: Scripture Psalm 46:1–7 NIV Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
Change can be difficult. Sometimes it is not even the change itself that is hardest, but the uncertainty that comes with it. We might know how yesterday worked, but suddenly we are not quite sure what tomorrow will look like.
That can happen when we start somewhere new, perhaps a new school, class or group. We need to learn where we fit, who people are and how things work. But change can happen in familiar places too. Someone we know might begin behaving differently towards us. A friendship might feel different. Something that once seemed easy can suddenly become confusing, and we can find ourselves wondering what we are supposed to do next.
The Bible never promises us a life where nothing changes. In fact, many of the people we read about in Scripture found themselves facing enormous uncertainty. Abraham left the place he knew without knowing exactly where God was taking him. Joseph’s whole life changed when his brothers sold him into slavery. Ruth left her home and began again in a foreign land. David went from looking after sheep, to living in a palace, to running for his life. The disciples left their old lives to follow Jesus, often without knowing what the next day would bring.
What they discovered — and what we can discover too — is that when everything around us changes, God does not.
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
— Hebrews 13:8
The Psalms often describe God as a rock. A rock is strong and steady. It does not move simply because the wind blows or the weather changes.
“The Lord is my rock, my fortress and my deliverer; my God is my rock, in whom I take refuge.”
— Psalm 18:2
That does not mean we will always immediately understand what is happening. Sometimes we would like God to show us exactly how everything is going to work out. We want a map of the whole journey: Who will my friends be? Will I enjoy this? Why is that person acting differently? What happens next?
But Scripture gives us another picture:
“Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.”
— Psalm 119:105
A lamp carried on a dark path does not normally show you everything several miles ahead. It shows you the ground in front of you. You can see enough to take the next step.
Sometimes that is how God leads us. He does not give us every answer at once. Instead, He asks us to trust Him today: to choose kindness today, to have courage today, to tell the truth today, to forgive today, to ask for help today. Then tomorrow, He gives us light for the next step.
Proverbs gives us a similar encouragement:
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.”
— Proverbs 3:5–6
Notice that it does not say we will always understand the path. It says we can trust God as we walk it.
This is especially important when other people change. We cannot control what somebody else thinks, says or does. We cannot force another person to remain the same. But we can ask God to help us decide how we will respond. We can still be kind without allowing someone to treat us badly. We can still forgive while asking a parent, teacher or trusted adult for help. We can be patient when someone is having a difficult time, while remembering that their choices do not have to determine ours.
And when we feel unsettled, God invites us to bring that uncertainty to Him.
“God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear…”
— Psalm 46:1–2
Things around us will change many times during our lives. Schools change. Friendships change. Families grow. Plans change. We grow and change too. Some changes will be exciting and others will be difficult.
But underneath all of those things is something that does not move.
God is still God. He is still good. He is still with us. His Word is still a light for our path, and He is still our rock.
So when we cannot see the whole road ahead, perhaps we do not need to.
We can ask a simpler question:
“God, what is the next right step you are asking me to take?”
And then, holding onto Him, we take it.
Talk about it # Is there anything changing at the moment that feels exciting, difficult or uncertain? When something changes, what are you most likely to worry about? Why do you think the Bible describes God as a rock? What might it mean for God’s Word to be a lamp rather than a floodlight showing us everything ahead? Is there one “next right step” you think God might be asking you to take this week? Things to remember # Psalm 46 describes a world where even the earth and mountains seem to move, yet God remains a safe place in the middle of it all. Psalm 119 gives us another picture: God’s word is a lamp for our feet. We do not need to see the whole journey before we can trust Him with the next step.
Important message # When everything around us changes, God does not. We can trust Him for the next step even when we cannot see the whole road ahead.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you do not change even when the world around us does. When we are excited about something new, help us to enjoy it with you. When we feel unsure or frightened, remind us that you are our rock and our safe place.
Help us not to worry because we cannot see the whole road ahead. Give us enough light for the next step. Give us wisdom when friendships or circumstances change, courage when things feel unfamiliar, and kindness in the way we respond to other people.
Help us to trust you with all our hearts and to remember that wherever we go, you go with us.
Amen.

You might move to a new class. Someone might start playing with different friends. A place that used to feel easy might suddenly feel strange. When that happens, it can make your tummy feel funny or make you wonder, “What do I do now?”
The Bible tells us something very important: God does not change.
He is like a big, strong rock that does not move when everything around it feels wobbly.
The Bible also tells us that God’s word is like a lamp for our feet. Imagine walking outside when it is very dark and you have a little torch. You might not be able to see all the way to the end of the road, but you can see enough to take the next step.
That is sometimes how God helps us. We might not know everything that is going to happen tomorrow, but we can ask Him to help us with today.

God can help us like that. We can trust Him one step at a time.

Read: Scripture Psalm 46:1–7 NIV Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
Change can be difficult. Sometimes it is not even the change itself that is hardest, but the uncertainty that comes with it. We might know how yesterday worked, but suddenly we are not quite sure what tomorrow will look like.
That can happen when we start somewhere new, perhaps a new school, class or group. We need to learn where we fit, who people are and how things work. But change can happen in familiar places too. Someone we know might begin behaving differently towards us. A friendship might feel different. Something that once seemed easy can suddenly become confusing, and we can find ourselves wondering what we are supposed to do next.
title: When Things Change

content:
Over the last few weeks I’ve been writing more.
That has created a slightly unexpected problem.
Writing the article itself was never really the whole problem. I needed somewhere for ideas to start, somewhere they could develop, somewhere finished thinking could live, and a sensible way of sharing it.
For a while those things were all getting mixed together.
I had notes in Obsidian. Drafts developed through conversations. Articles on LinkedIn. Older posts elsewhere. Ideas that were clearly related to one another but were effectively trapped inside individual documents.
What I realised was that I didn’t really need a blogging platform.
I needed a publishing system.
That distinction feels familiar. When I wrote recently about the personal system I use to manage notes, tasks and ADHD, the useful part was never really the choice of tools. It was understanding the problem I was trying to solve, noticing where the friction actually was, and then giving the different parts of the system clear jobs.
I’ve ended up doing much the same thing with writing.
Separating thinking from publishing # Obsidian has become increasingly important to how I work.
It is where incomplete thoughts are allowed to remain incomplete.
An article might start with a sentence, an observation from a client conversation, a diagram, or something that has irritated me enough that I want to understand why.
As I develop it, I want to keep the bits that don’t eventually make the article too: alternative arguments, examples, questions, links to other ideas and things that probably deserve their own article later.
That makes Obsidian a very good knowledge base.
It doesn’t necessarily make it the thing I want to publish.
That distinction turned out to be important.
My working notes should optimise for thinking.
The published version should optimise for reading.
Trying to make one file perfectly fulfil both purposes creates some odd compromises.
A deliberate path from thought to publication # Once I separated those concerns, the publishing flow became much simpler.
flowchart LR A[ObsidianThinking, research and drafts] B[GitHubPublic content source] C[HugoBuilds the site] D[GitHub PagesPublishes the site] E[LinkedInDistribution and conversation] A -->|article is ready| B B --> C C --> D D -->|selected ideas travel to| EThe point isn’t sophistication. It is creating a clear path from a working thought to a published article without making the mechanics heavier than the writing itself.
Git felt like a natural boundary # Once I started thinking about the published article as a separate artefact, GitHub began to make much more sense.
I’ve spent enough of my career around software engineering that source control feels like a fairly natural way of managing something that evolves.
An article has a history.
It changes.
Sometimes I make a small correction. Sometimes an argument develops substantially. Sometimes several related pieces start emerging from the same original thought.
Git gives me a simple record of that without needing to invent another content-management process.
More importantly, committing something creates a useful boundary.
There is a difference between an idea I am still developing in Obsidian and something I am prepared to put into a public repository as part of my published body of work.
That little bit of friction is actually useful.
Why Hugo? # I looked again at conventional blogging platforms, but most of them solve a slightly different problem.
They are very good at providing an interface for creating web content.
I already have an interface for creating content.
It is Obsidian, Markdown and increasingly the tools around my own knowledge base.
What I wanted from the website was therefore relatively modest.
Take Markdown.
Turn it into a fast, simple site.
Give the content enough structure that I can connect things over time.
Stay out of the way.
Hugo fits that model extremely well.
An article is essentially a Markdown file with some metadata around it: title, date, description, categories and some information about how it connects to the rest of the site.
The website itself can then be rebuilt from those files whenever something changes.
There isn’t really a database of articles sitting behind it. The repository is the content.
I like that.
GitHub Pages closes the loop # The final technical piece is GitHub Pages.
The deployment is automated through GitHub Actions. I commit the article, Hugo builds the site, and GitHub Pages publishes the result.
There are obviously many technically more sophisticated architectures I could build.
That isn’t really the point.
The goal is to make publishing cheap enough, cognitively as much as financially, that the tooling doesn’t become another reason not to write.
This is also an interesting evolution of something I was already doing several years ago. I wrote about automating Hugo deployment with GitHub Actions in 2022. The mechanics have changed since then, but the instinct is the same: automate the repetitive part and preserve attention for the part that needs thought.
Giving each platform one job # The more important shift was deciding that each platform had a different job.
flowchart LR A[Obsidian] -->|optimises for| A1[Thinking] B[Hugo site] -->|optimises for| B1[Reading] C[LinkedIn] -->|optimises for| C1[Conversation]That sounds almost trivial written down, but it removed quite a lot of ambiguity.
Obsidian is where the idea is developed and connected to other thinking.
The Hugo site is the durable public version.
LinkedIn is useful for reach, discussion and putting an idea in front of people I already know or who are working on similar problems.
LinkedIn therefore isn’t where I want my writing to live.
It is where I want some of it to travel.
That feels healthier than treating every platform as another place that must contain another identical copy.
A small content operating model # This is probably why the setup feels familiar to me.
I’ve spent a lot of my career thinking about flow, architecture and operating models.
One of the recurring mistakes in all three is allowing the tools or organisational boundaries to define the process.
We buy a system and then gradually reshape the work around what the system expects.
I’m trying to do the opposite here.
Each component has a fairly explicit responsibility.
Obsidian optimises for thinking and connections.
Git provides history and a deliberate publication boundary.
Hugo turns structured content into the public site.
GitHub Pages handles delivery.
LinkedIn provides distribution and conversation.
None of those tools needs to own the entire process.
It is essentially a very small content operating model built around separation of concerns.
Building a body of thinking # There is another reason I’ve wanted to do this.
I don’t particularly want to build a collection of posts.
I want to build a connected body of thinking.
Some of the ideas I’m writing about now have existed in different forms throughout my career. Others are developing very quickly as AI changes what is possible in software, organisations and decision-making.
Those relationships matter.
graph TD Flow[Flow] Dependencies[Dependencies] Horizons[Horizons] Guardrails[Guardrails] Context[Enterprise context] KG[Knowledge graphs] Decisioning[Decision-making] Agency[Agency] VSM[Value streams] OperatingModels[Operating models] OperatingModels --> Flow Flow --> Dependencies Dependencies --> Horizons Horizons --> Guardrails Flow --> VSM VSM --> Decisioning Context --> KG KG --> Decisioning Decisioning --> Agency Context --> OperatingModelsA reader arriving because of something I’ve written about AI should eventually be able to follow the connections into enterprise context, decision-making, knowledge graphs and agency.
Someone reading about transformation might move through flow, dependencies, constraints, horizons and guardrails.
And my own working notes can contain far richer connections than I would ever expose directly on the website.
The public article becomes one expression of a much larger knowledge graph.
That is the direction I find particularly interesting.
The system will probably keep changing # The system I use today almost certainly isn’t the one I’ll be using in a year’s time.
That was one of the lessons from building my personal operating system too.
The objective isn’t to discover the perfect toolchain.
It is to notice the friction, understand what is causing it, and adjust the system.
Right now GitHub, Hugo and GitHub Pages give me something quite simple: ownership of the content, a durable public home, version history, an automated publishing path and enough structure to begin connecting ideas properly.
Obsidian gives me somewhere for those ideas to remain messy before they become articles.
And LinkedIn gives me somewhere to have the conversation afterwards.
The technology is useful.
But the more important change has been deciding that thinking, publishing and distribution are different activities.
Once I separated those, the technology choices became surprisingly straightforward.

content:
One of the more difficult problems I keep coming back to with AI-assisted software modernisation isn’t really a technology problem. It’s trust.
We have all seen an LLM confidently make something up, merge two facts that happened to look similar, or produce an explanation that sounds entirely reasonable until someone who really understands the domain reads it. Once you have seen that happen a few times, it changes how you approach the capability, and that matters when we start asking AI to help modernise software.
The obvious response is control. If we don’t completely trust the generated code, we review it. If we don’t completely trust the generated specification, we review that too. Perhaps we generate a specification from the legacy application, have somebody approve it, generate new code from the approved specification, generate tests, review those, and then put the normal release controls around the resulting system.
Individually, every one of those steps is reasonable. Collectively, though, there is a risk that we recreate exactly the sort of delivery pipeline we have spent the last decade trying to simplify.
Moving the bottleneck # There is a familiar pattern here from software delivery. When release processes were slow, organisations often responded by adding more people to release management, more coordination, more checklists and more approvals. Sometimes that helped. Sometimes it simply made the process around the constraint larger without really changing the constraint itself.
AI modernisation can create a similar problem.
Imagine using AI to analyse a large legacy estate and generate detailed specifications for thousands of components. The generation itself may be extraordinarily fast, but somebody still has to decide whether the output is good enough to act on.
If every generated specification has to be read and approved before we trust it, then the AI may have created work faster than the organisation is capable of consuming it. The bottleneck has not disappeared; it has shifted from producing the specification to verifying it.
That starts to change the economics of the approach.
We can put humans in the loop at every stage: specification, design, code, tests and release. That may reduce some forms of risk, but it can also absorb much of the time advantage we hoped to gain in the first place.
I’ve written previously about the tendency to add human approval when what we really need may be a better guardrail. The same tension shows up here. The issue is not that review is unnecessary. It is that we need to be clearer about what the review is intended to establish.
Code-to-code isn’t necessarily modernisation # There is another temptation here. If generating and reviewing specifications becomes expensive, why not simply transform the old code directly into new code?
That can work technically, but modernisation usually exists because something about the old system no longer fits the environment in which it needs to operate.
Legacy systems accumulate assumptions: architectural patterns suited to older deployment models, batch processes that made sense when compute was scarce, tight coupling that evolved over years, interfaces shaped around organisational boundaries that no longer exist, and business rules mixed with implementation detail.
A sufficiently capable model may be able to translate that faithfully from one language or framework into another. The difficulty is that fidelity is not always the goal.
A highly accurate code-to-code transformation can still preserve the architectural and design decisions that made the system difficult to operate in the first place. The syntax is modern, but the system may not really be.
In some ways, this creates an uncomfortable trade-off. The more freedom we give the AI to reinterpret what the legacy application was actually trying to achieve, the more useful its judgement may become. At the same time, the more freedom we give it, the less deterministic the result becomes, and the harder it is to establish confidence in the output.
The constraint may be trust # This is where I think the problem becomes more interesting.
Perhaps the main constraint in AI-enabled modernisation is not generation capacity at all. Perhaps it is trust.
A client may not fully trust the AI-generated output. A delivery team may, in some cases, trust it too readily, particularly when the model is operating in a part of the domain where they are less experienced themselves. Both responses are understandable, and both carry risk.
Low trust tends to create gates, approvals and verification. Excessive trust creates the possibility of accepting something because it is plausible rather than because it is correct.
Our traditional delivery mechanisms are not especially well suited to this tension. Software systems have generally been treated as deterministic things: given the same input and the same state, we expect broadly the same behaviour.
Large language models are different. They are probabilistic systems that can exhibit something closer to judgement than traditional software, and that changes the nature of the control problem.
I increasingly wonder whether some of the difficulty we have applying AI inside organisations comes from trying to operate a non-deterministic capability using control mechanisms designed for deterministic systems.
What are we actually reviewing? # That raises a more fundamental question about what we are trying to validate.
Our instinct is usually to validate the artefact: read the specification, review the code, check the generated tests, approve the document.
But an AI-assisted modernisation system is not just the model. The effective system is something closer to:
model + context + memory + tools + constraints + evaluation
Change the context and the behaviour changes. Change the available memory and the behaviour changes. Change the retrieval strategy, system instructions or tools and the behaviour changes again.
If that is the real system, validating thousands of individual documents may not always be the most useful level of abstraction.
We don’t normally gain confidence in a compiler by manually reviewing every line of machine code it generates. AI is not equivalent to a compiler, of course, and its non-determinism is exactly what makes this harder. But there may still be something useful in the comparison.
Rather than asking only whether every generated specification is correct, perhaps we should also be asking how well the system understands the application.
That shifts the nature of assurance.
Can it explain why a particular business rule exists? Can it identify contradictions between implementations? Can it trace a behaviour from interface through application logic into data? Can it distinguish an implementation detail from genuine business intent? Can it show what evidence led it to a conclusion? Can an expert challenge that conclusion and see whether the underlying understanding holds up?
This starts to look less like document review and more like testing the quality of the system’s understanding.
Interviewing understanding # That language feels unusual when applied to software, but perhaps that is useful in itself.
If the real value of these systems is their ability to reason across large amounts of messy context, then evaluating them only through generated documents may not tell us enough about whether that reasoning is sound.
Take a legacy trading platform as an example. Rather than generating a 900-page specification and asking somebody to approve it from beginning to end, the modernisation team might interrogate the system’s understanding of the estate.
Which business capabilities appear to be critical? Which calculations are repeated across multiple implementations? Where are the contradictory rules? Which behaviours appear intentional and which look like implementation artefacts? What happens if a particular upstream feed is unavailable? Where else does this concept appear? What evidence supports this interpretation?
That is a different kind of interaction. It gives experienced people the opportunity to test relationships, assumptions and reasoning, rather than simply proofreading a very large body of generated text.
For me, that feels closer to the way trust may need to develop.
Guardrails and judgement # There is still an important tension here.
The more tightly we constrain these systems, the more predictable they become. That is useful, but beyond a point the same constraints can also reduce the judgement that made the AI useful in the first place.
If we force the model to perform only deterministic transformations, we can probably make the output easier to verify. We may also reduce the capability to little more than a sophisticated translation engine.
Modernisation often needs more than translation. It may require recognising that two differently named things are really the same business concept, noticing that a technical implementation no longer reflects the way the organisation operates, distinguishing an architectural constraint from an accident of history, or deciding that something should not be carried forward at all.
Those are judgement calls, and they are harder to express through simple binary controls.
So the goal may not be to remove non-determinism entirely. It may be to become much more deliberate about where it is useful, where it is acceptable, and how we build confidence around it.
A different operating model # That is why I think the more interesting question around AI modernisation is becoming less about the model itself and more about the operating model around it.
There will still be places where deterministic behaviour matters, places where individual outputs need to be checked, and places where traditional controls remain entirely appropriate.
But there may also be places where confidence comes from something broader: the quality of the context, the traceability of conclusions, the ability to challenge the system’s reasoning, and the consistency of its understanding across a wider body of evidence.
That makes trust less of a single approval decision and more of something that has to be designed into the system.
AI can generate code extraordinarily quickly. It can generate documentation even faster. Neither matters very much if the organisation cannot build enough confidence in the result to act on it.
If trust is the real constraint, generating more artefacts probably will not solve it. The harder question is how we design the technical and organisational system around the AI so that trust can develop without recreating the very bottlenecks we were trying to remove.

content:
“Human in the loop” has become one of the standard answers to concerns about AI. We do not entirely trust the model, so we put a person somewhere in the process to validate what it has done. On the surface that sounds sensible, and sometimes it absolutely is.
But I think it exposes a much older problem in the way we design controls.
I’ve spent a lot of time working with security and compliance teams, and more recently with OT security teams where getting controls wrong can affect physical assets and operations as well as systems and data. I’ve seen similar patterns in higher education and charities, where safeguarding, accountability and practicality have to coexist across both physical and digital boundaries.
Across all of those environments, one question has become increasingly useful: what decision are we actually asking the human to make? The presence of a person does not, by itself, create judgement. Sometimes we are asking someone to weigh incomplete information and competing risks. Sometimes we are asking them to provide context that the system does not have. And sometimes we are simply asking a person to execute a set of deterministic rules that could have been encoded in the control itself. We tend to call all three “approval”. They are not the same thing.
Take IAM approvals. If someone is deciding whether access is permitted based on a known role, a defined system, segregation-of-duties rules, data classification and a clear policy, then there may be very little judgement involved. In that case the process is really applying policy. A person may still be sitting in the loop, but the decision itself is largely deterministic.
That is very different from a manager being asked whether someone genuinely needs the access to do their job. The policy may tell us that the access is allowable, but the manager is supplying business context. A security team may then be looking at a different question again: does granting the access introduce a technical or regulatory risk that is not obvious from the role alone? Those are three different decisions, yet we often hide them inside one workflow labelled “approval”.
That is where I think a lot of control design starts to go wrong. We focus on the presence of an approver rather than the anatomy of the decision.
A useful way to think about this is as a spectrum. At one end are deterministic decisions, where the answer follows from known rules and available facts. If a request complies with a defined policy, there may be no value in asking a person to reproduce the same calculation manually. There may still be exceptions, but the normal path should not require judgement.
Then there are contextual decisions. The rules still matter, but they are not enough on their own. Someone needs to understand the situation, interpret additional information, or decide whether something that is technically permissible actually makes sense. Good tooling can help gather the facts, identify anomalies and present the relevant context rather than simply presenting another yes/no button.
Beyond that are judgement-based decisions. These involve uncertainty, competing objectives or risks that cannot be reduced to a simple rule. The answer may not be yes or no. It may be “proceed with an additional control”, “accept the risk temporarily”, “choose a different route”, or “we need more information before deciding”. That is genuine judgement because someone is weighing consequences rather than checking compliance with a predefined rule.
And then there are decisions that are collective or contested. A decision may be acceptable from a delivery perspective but unacceptable from an operational, safety or regulatory perspective. In those cases the problem is not simply that we need more approvers. We need clarity about who owns which risk, who has the right to decide, and how conflicts are resolved when two legitimate perspectives point in different directions.
That “who” question is important and, I think, often overlooked. Why is this person the approver? Do they own the risk? Do they understand the context? Are they accountable for the outcome, or are they simply in the workflow because the process needed someone to click approve?
If the decision is deterministic, putting a senior person in the loop does not make it more valuable. If the decision requires business context, sending it to a central control team may be equally weak because they may not have the information needed to make a meaningful call. The right question is not just whether a human is present, but whether the right person is making the right kind of decision with the right information.
A simple example everyone loves to hate is expenses. Most organisations have some version of the same process: submit a receipt, select a category, confirm that the spend is within policy, then send it to someone else to approve. If the amount is within a known limit, the category is permitted, the receipt is present and there are no obvious anomalies, what is the manager actually being asked to judge? Often, very little. Yet we still create queues, reminders, dashboards and escalation processes around that approval step, and then measure how quickly managers clear them. We become very efficient at processing a queue that perhaps should not exist in the first place.
There is also a psychological risk in the way we design these controls. If someone is repeatedly presented with a long list of simple yes/no decisions, particularly where the reason for the control is unclear, the natural behaviour is to process the list rather than think deeply about each decision. Mental fatigue plays a part, but so does meaning. If people cannot see the value in the decision they are being asked to make, it quickly becomes an administrative task rather than an exercise in judgement.
That changes behaviour. Some people will rubber-stamp because approving is the quickest way to clear the queue. Others will become overly cautious because saying “no” feels safer than taking responsibility for a decision. In the worst cases, a control function can begin to behave like a no factory: its visible output becomes the number of things it has stopped rather than the risks it has intelligently managed.
Measurement can reinforce this. Activity is much easier to count than outcome. We can measure approvals completed, requests rejected, reviews performed and queue times. It is much harder to measure whether the organisation is now safer, whether the control prevented a meaningful risk, or whether the same outcome could have been achieved with less friction.
Once activity becomes the measure, activity has a habit of becoming the goal. Teams optimise for processing more approvals, identifying more exceptions, or demonstrating that controls are being exercised. Taken far enough, there is even a danger that the system implicitly expects a certain number of “no” decisions simply to demonstrate that the control is working. That is classic local optimisation: the control function may look highly effective while the overall system becomes slower, less engaged and not necessarily any safer.
The better question is not how much control activity we performed, but whether the control reduced risk while preserving the flow of value. That requires a more mature conversation about outcomes, decision rights and the nature of the risk being managed.
This is one of the reasons I think there is a useful lesson to carry forward from DevOps and modern security engineering. The goal was never to remove controls; it was to stop treating every control as a manual interruption. Where the rules were clear, we increasingly encoded them. Where the boundary was known, we built guardrails around it. Where something moved outside that boundary, we surfaced it to someone who had the context and authority to make a real decision.
That creates a much healthier relationship between safety and flow. Safety does not have to mean slowing everything down. Done well, the control becomes part of the flow rather than a queue sitting outside it.
This brings me back to AI. As we build AI-enabled and increasingly agentic systems, trust and validation are becoming central design questions. “Put a human in the loop” is an understandable response, but it is not enough to tell us whether the system is well controlled. Before adding another human checkpoint, we should model the decision itself: what evidence is required, which parts are deterministic, what context needs to be understood, whether there is a genuine trade-off to weigh, who owns the risk, who has the authority to accept it, and whether this is one person’s decision at all.
AI can help across several of those layers, but that does not mean it should replace every form of automation. Where a decision is deterministic, the best answer may still be a conventional rules engine, workflow, policy-as-code check or other established automation. If we know that the same inputs should always produce the same answer, there is little value in introducing a non-deterministic model into that part of the process.
AI becomes more useful where context needs to be gathered, interpreted or summarised; where anomalies need to be identified; where the relevant evidence is spread across multiple systems; or where a recommendation needs to be formed from information that is harder to express as a fixed rule. In many cases the strongest design will therefore be a combination: deterministic tools enforcing the boundaries we understand, AI helping to assemble and interpret context, and people making the decisions that genuinely require judgement.
The AI may orchestrate or call those existing tools rather than replace them. An agent might invoke a policy engine, query an identity platform, run a calculation or trigger an established workflow, then use the results to decide what should happen next or what needs to be surfaced to a person. That separation matters for trust as well as efficiency. We should not ask a probabilistic model to reproduce a deterministic control simply because AI happens to be the newest component in the architecture.
The objective should not be to maximise either automation or human involvement. It should be to put each in the part of the decision where it adds value. That is ultimately what good guardrails do: they automate the boundaries we understand so that we can spend human attention on the uncertainty we don’t.
Because every policy decision we ask a person to make steals attention from the judgement calls that only they can make.
summary:
“Human in the loop” has become one of the standard answers to concerns about AI. We do not entirely trust the model, so we put a person somewhere in the process to validate what it has done. On the surface that sounds sensible, and sometimes it absolutely is.
But I think it exposes a much older problem in the way we design controls.
I’ve spent a lot of time working with security and compliance teams, and more recently with OT security teams where getting controls wrong can affect physical assets and operations as well as systems and data. I’ve seen similar patterns in higher education and charities, where safeguarding, accountability and practicality have to coexist across both physical and digital boundaries.
title: Human in the loop isn’t the same as human judgement

I’ve been building a wall of shelves in my office.
Like most DIY jobs, it started with a fairly simple picture in my head and rapidly became a network of dependencies. I couldn’t cut a shelf accurately until the uprights were fixed. I couldn’t fix the next section until I knew how the previous one actually sat against a wall that was considerably less straight than it looked. Some pieces could be measured once and reproduced. Others genuinely had to wait until something else was complete.
Somewhere between measuring another piece of timber and walking back to the saw, I realised there was a familiar organisational problem hiding in it.
We talk a lot in business about managing dependencies. Managing them matters. But I’m increasingly convinced it is the wrong starting point.
A dependency isn’t simply something to put on a RAID log, represent with a line on a programme plan, or discuss at the next coordination meeting. It is part of the design of the system.
And this becomes particularly visible as organisations move towards a product operating model — a journey many of my clients are currently on. Persistent teams with clearer ownership are very good at exposing where the real boundaries are. Once a team genuinely owns an outcome rather than a temporary slice of a programme, the repeated journeys outside that team become much easier to see:
The same security review every release The same infrastructure request The same architecture decision The same data dependency The same team waiting for another team before it can move Those dependencies were often there before. A product model simply makes them harder to hide inside a programme plan.
And broadly, I think there are only three ways to deal with them.
1. Bring it close # The first option is proximity.
If one team is constantly dependent on a particular skill, capability or decision, bring that capability into the team. Embed the security engineer. Put an architect into the product team. Bring the data expertise closer. Create the multidisciplinary team rather than making people repeatedly cross organisational boundaries to get work done.
In the office, this was the equivalent of moving the tools to where I was working. If every adjustment meant walking somewhere else, setting something up, making a cut and returning to see whether it fitted, the transaction cost rapidly became greater than the work itself.
The same happens inside organisations. Sometimes we call this collaboration, but structurally what we have actually done is shortened the dependency. This is often the right answer when the work is ambiguous, highly interactive or changing quickly. It also fits naturally with product thinking: give the team more of the capabilities it needs to own the outcome rather than just its part of the process.
The downside is obvious: you cannot embed every specialist everywhere. Which leads to the second option.
2. Productise it # If bringing the dependency into the team doesn’t scale, turn the capability into a product.
Define the interface. Make the request predictable. Create a service level. Better still, make it self-service.
This is the journey from:
“Speak to Dave in the infrastructure team.”
To:
“Raise this form and somebody will provision it.”
And eventually:
“Choose what you need from the catalogue and it will be provisioned automatically.”
That is much more than automation. It is changing the nature of the relationship.
The dependency moves from white glove to autonomous.
Back at the shelves, once I had worked out a dimension that repeated, I stopped treating every piece as a new problem. I could use the same measurement, the same setup and the same process. The thinking had been turned into a repeatable interface.
This is one of the reasons good platform engineering fits so naturally into a product operating model. A platform team should not simply be a central team that other product teams queue up to talk to. At its best, it takes a recurring organisational dependency and turns it into a product that can be consumed with as little coordination as possible.
The dependency still exists.
The conversation does not have to.
3. Synchronise it # And then there is the difficult one.
Sometimes the dependency cannot sensibly be embedded. It cannot be abstracted behind an interface. The two pieces of work genuinely have to meet. In that case, you have to synchronise.
Plans need to align. Priorities need to align. Capacity needs to be available at roughly the same time. Decisions made by one group need to arrive before another group reaches the point where they are required.
This sounds straightforward on a programme plan. It is anything but. Synchronisation requires two independently operating systems to remain aligned over time, and the moment priorities change in one of them, the dependency starts to drift.
This gets particularly interesting in a product organisation. If two persistent product teams need to constantly coordinate their roadmaps in order to deliver value, then the dependency itself deserves attention.
Perhaps:
The team boundary is wrong A shared capability should be productised There really is a genuine business dependency that needs synchronisation But the answer should not automatically be another cross-team meeting.
This is why I think synchronisation should often be the last choice, rather than the default one. Organisations frequently respond to dependencies by adding coordination: more planning, more governance, more meetings, more programme management. Sometimes that is necessary, but sometimes we are applying coordination to a dependency that should have been redesigned.
Product models expose the joins # One of the useful things about moving towards a product operating model is that it exposes the joins in the organisation.
A project structure can sometimes mask them. A programme manager can chase an action. A delivery plan can contain an assumption. A milestone can move. A dependency can remain visible as a line on a slide without anyone questioning why it exists in the first place.
Persistent product teams make that harder. If the same dependency appears sprint after sprint, quarter after quarter, it starts to tell you something — not just about delivery, but about the operating model.
So when I see a team waiting on another team, I’m trying to ask a different set of questions:
Can we bring the capability closer? Can we productise the interaction? Or do these teams genuinely need to synchronise? Those choices have very different implications.
Bring it close when the interaction is rich and frequent. Productise it when the interaction can be made predictable and repeatable. Synchronise when the work genuinely has to converge.
And perhaps most importantly, don’t confuse synchronisation with dependency management in general. Because if your organisation needs a meeting every week to keep two teams aligned, that might be good coordination. But it might also be telling you something about the way the system has been designed.
Dependencies are inevitable.
A good product operating model helps you see them.
What you do with them is a design choice.
