I have been doing a lot of experimentation with local models recently, as have many of my colleagues. There is also a growing anticipation around the next generation of developer workstations and AI-focused boxes: machines capable of running increasingly useful models without sending every request to a SaaS platform.
It is easy to see this as another technology choice: local versus cloud, open model versus proprietary model, workstation versus API. I think the more interesting question for enterprises is economic.
For years, we have invested in developer productivity up front. Powerful laptops and desktops, good monitors, fast build environments and development infrastructure are accepted as part of the cost of enabling people to do their jobs. We do not ask an engineer to demonstrate the business value of every compile before allowing them to run it.
AI has pushed us towards a rather different model.
Every prompt has a cost. Every experiment consumes tokens. At small scale that is relatively easy to ignore, but across a large organisation the uncertainty quickly becomes uncomfortable. If we expect thousands of technical people to use these capabilities continuously, a variable pay-per-use model creates a very different fiscal problem.
The understandable response is governance. Quotas appear. Access is restricted. Teams are asked to justify use cases before experimenting with them. Someone wants to understand the likely return before approving the spend.
All of those things can look fiscally responsible. They can also create exactly the wrong behaviour.
The marginal cost of curiosity # There is an interesting alternative emerging.
What if we treated some AI capability in the same way we treat the developer workstation?
A deliberately higher capital investment — perhaps several thousand pounds more for a developer machine capable of running useful models locally — can look expensive when compared with buying a cheaper laptop. But that is not necessarily the right comparison.
The comparison is between the capital cost of providing reasoning capacity and the ongoing cost of purchasing that capacity by the token.
If our starting assumption is that AI becomes part of the normal technical toolkit, rather than an occasional specialist service, then pre-allocating some of that capacity starts to make sense.
It changes the economics of experimentation too.
Once the machine has been bought, the marginal financial cost of asking another question, trying another approach, generating another test or exploring another idea becomes close to zero. The investment has already been made.
That matters because experimentation is inherently uncertain. If we already knew which experiments would create value, they would not really be experiments.
A funding model that requires teams to demonstrate the value of every possible use before consuming the capability risks suppressing the exploration required to discover that value in the first place.
For the CFO, there is another useful characteristic: predictability.
A known capital allocation to developer capability is much easier to plan than an uncertain curve of token consumption that may accelerate rapidly as adoption grows. This does not make local compute free, of course. Hardware, electricity, support, model management and refresh cycles all have costs. But they are costs we already know how to reason about.
The aim is not simply to make AI cheaper. It is to reduce the cost — and the organisational friction — of curiosity.
The security argument follows the economics # Cost is only one part of this.
A significant amount of enterprise AI governance currently focuses on questions such as model choice, data egress, security boundaries and sovereignty. Those concerns are becoming more important, particularly for organisations operating across regulated industries and multiple jurisdictions.
Enterprise-controlled models change some of that conversation.
If a useful class of experimentation can happen on infrastructure the organisation controls, then we know much more clearly where the data is being processed, what can leave the environment and which models are available. The reasoning capability sits inside a boundary we already understand rather than requiring every exploratory use case to cross into an external sandbox or SaaS service.
That does not remove the need for governance. Models still need to be selected, patched, evaluated and controlled. Sensitive information still needs appropriate handling. Local execution is not automatically safe execution.
But it can make the security and sovereignty model substantially easier to reason about.
More importantly, it can create confidence for teams working with problems they would otherwise be reluctant to explore with an external service.
I increasingly think AI workbench is a more useful mental model than AI sandbox.
A sandbox sounds temporary: somewhere we are allowed to play before doing the real work elsewhere. A workbench is part of the normal environment. It is equipped, controlled and expected to be used continuously.
Not everything belongs locally # None of this suggests that every workload should run on a local or enterprise-controlled model.
The frontier SaaS models remain extraordinarily useful. For some problems the additional reasoning capability will easily justify the cost. Other workloads need scale or capabilities that make centralised services the obvious choice.
The architecture therefore becomes a portfolio rather than a binary decision.
Some reasoning capacity can be provisioned as a predictable enterprise capability. Some can be consumed on demand. Some workloads may never be permitted to leave a particular boundary. Others may deliberately use premium external models because the potential value of the question dwarfs the cost of answering it.
That leads to another problem I find particularly interesting: routing.
Most model routers look at the question being asked and try to infer how capable a model is required to answer it. But the complexity of a question is not the same as its value.
A technically simple question might influence a decision worth millions. A complicated piece of analysis might be little more than experimentation.
How do we know the difference before the question has been answered?
I suspect this becomes less of a reasoning problem and more of a context and memory problem. If the system understands who is asking, what they are working on, which business capability or decision the work supports, the sensitivity of the information involved and the consequences of getting it wrong, then model selection can become an economic and governance decision rather than simply a technical one.
That connects directly to the wider challenge of enterprise context. The more agency we give these systems, the more important the surrounding knowledge, decision structures and guardrails become.
Capacity, not tokens # There is a temptation to treat AI consumption as something entirely new. In some respects it is. But enterprises have dealt with variations of this problem before.
We invest in capacity where we expect sustained use. We consume services where elasticity or specialist capability creates more value. And we build governance around the boundary between the two.
The interesting shift may therefore be less about choosing between local models and SaaS models and more about deciding which reasoning capacity should become part of the standard enterprise environment.
If we believe AI is going to become an everyday part of technical work, then perhaps asking every experiment to justify its token bill is the wrong fiscal model.
The goal should be to create an environment where experimentation is affordable, secure and sovereign enough to happen routinely — while still giving people access to more capable services when the value of the work justifies them.
That feels less like buying AI and more like designing an organisation in which curiosity has somewhere safe to happen.

I was chatting recently with someone else who has ADHD about how I manage notes, tasks and to-dos. What surprised me was that the useful bit wasn’t really the tools. It was the process I’d gone through to get there.
I was diagnosed with ADHD relatively recently, and that gave me a useful lens for understanding why some of my productivity systems had worked for a while and then gradually collapsed under their own weight. I don’t want to dwell on the diagnosis itself here. What mattered was the reframing.
I realised I didn’t really have a problem with capturing things. If anything, I could capture too much: notes, actions, ideas, follow-ups, things to research, things I ought to do and things I might want to do later.
All of it could be safely stored somewhere. The problem was that a complete system was not necessarily a useful system.
The productivity version of too much WIP # This is where I started to notice a connection with some of the organisational principles I use in technology delivery.
In DevOps, Lean and flow-based delivery, we spend a lot of time worrying about work in progress.
Too much WIP creates queues. Queues create delay. Delay hides problems.
And once there is too much work in the system, starting more work often feels productive while actually making flow worse.
My personal task system was doing exactly the same thing. I had built an increasingly accurate inventory of everything I had not done. Tasks could remain open indefinitely. Old priorities sat alongside new ones, and things that had once mattered stayed visible long after the context had changed.
Because nothing was really forced out of the system, the list just became noisier. From a traditional task-management perspective, this was technically quite good: nothing was being forgotten. From an attention-management perspective, it was terrible.
The first improvement was not better organisation # One of the earliest changes I made was simply reducing the friction of capture.
I started using ChatGPT as a live note-taking layer. That meant I could capture things quickly and structure them afterwards rather than trying to listen, think, interpret, organise and document everything at the same time. That was useful in meetings, sermons, workshops and research.
Capture first. Structure later.
That eventually evolved into Obsidian becoming the durable knowledge layer, with Git underneath it and ChatGPT increasingly acting as the authoring and processing interface.
That part worked well. But it solved knowledge better than it solved attention.
Remembering everything turned out to be part of the problem # This was probably the more important realisation.
Knowledge benefits from persistence. Attention often does not.
I want decisions, context, notes and project history to survive. I do not necessarily want every task I have ever thought might be worth doing sitting in front of me every morning.
That distinction became increasingly important, and it led me back to one of the ideas from the Bullet Journal approach that I had probably underestimated before: migration.
Not migration as in copying yesterday’s unfinished tasks onto today’s page. Migration as a deliberate decision.
Do I still intend to do this? Is it still relevant? Does it belong to a project rather than today? Am I waiting on somebody else? Has the context changed? Can I just drop it? That is much closer to backlog refinement than task rollover.
Migration is really about re-establishing intent # This is the bit I now find most useful.
A task should not survive simply because I once wrote it down. It should survive because I still intend to do something about it.
That sounds obvious, but many digital task systems make persistence almost frictionless. Once something enters the backlog, it can live there forever. The result is the personal equivalent of an overloaded delivery pipeline: everything is in progress and nothing is really flowing.
So I now try to treat migration as a feedback loop: review the work, reassess the context, limit what is active, remove what no longer matters, then start again from a cleaner state.
That is very close to how I think about healthy engineering systems. Good flow is not created by pushing more work into the system. It comes from reducing queues, limiting WIP, making constraints visible and shortening the feedback loop.
The system I use now # What I’ve ended up with is less a productivity app and more a small personal operating model.
Obsidian holds durable knowledge, project context and history. Git gives me versioning and a reliable underlying store. ChatGPT acts as an interaction layer: capturing, structuring, reviewing and helping me reason about what is actually active.
Then there is a much lighter daily layer. That daily layer is intentionally disposable. Its job is not to represent everything; its job is to represent what deserves my attention now.
And periodically I migrate.
Not everything survives. That is a feature.
The principle underneath it # I think the most useful distinction I’ve arrived at is this:
Knowledge should persist. Attention should be disposable.
The knowledge system can be deep. The active work system should be shallow.
That separation has helped me far more than trying to build one perfect tool that remembers everything, prioritises everything and presents everything at once.
It also reflects something I’ve believed for a long time in organisational design. If work is not flowing, telling people to work harder is rarely the answer. You look at the system:
Where are the queues? Where is the cognitive load? Where are hand-offs creating friction? What work has entered the system without a clear exit? Where has “important” become indistinguishable from “still open”? That turns out to be a useful way to think about personal productivity too.
Design for recovery, not perfection # The other lesson is that the system needs to work when I am not operating at my best.
If a productivity system only works when I am highly organised, fully focused and consistently disciplined, it is not much of a system.
For me, the more useful design goal has become:
How quickly can I restart?
After a busy week. After travel. After getting distracted by something more interesting. After letting the task list drift. A good system should make recovery cheap.
That is probably the most DevOps-like principle of all. Don’t design for the assumption that nothing will go wrong. Design so that recovery is normal, fast and low-friction.
That is roughly where I have landed.
Not a perfect productivity system.
Just a set of feedback loops, constraints and external memory that make it easier for me to get back into flow.
A note on AI: I’ve used ChatGPT as part of the process of writing this article — mainly to help me reconstruct the journey, organise the notes and turn the thinking into a coherent draft. The underlying experiences, views and conclusions are mine.

I’ve always been a proponent of DevOps, and my recent experiments with Hugo have led me to automate the deployment of my site. This post details how I set up an automatic deployment process for my Hugo site using GitHub Actions while keeping my drafts and content private until I’m ready to share them.
Keeping a Private Repository for Hugo Site Definition # I have a private repository for my Hugo site definition to keep my draft posts and other content secure until they’re ready for the public. The objective was straightforward: whenever I commit changes to the main branch, Hugo runs, and the result is committed to another repository, specifically my GitHub Pages repo.
The Challenge of Automation # Although the process seems simple, it involved a few challenges I had to navigate through. Let me share my journey.
Utilizing GitHub Actions for CI # GitHub offers a robust CI tool with GitHub Actions. Actions operate using Docker containers that execute in sequence, and you can provide different parameters to each action. My goal was to have every commit to master built and published automatically.
Defining an Action in GitHub # An action in GitHub is defined in YAML, similar to many CI/CD tools. Here’s a breakdown of the components:
Naming the Workflow / Action
name: CI Setting the Trigger
on: push: branches: [master] Defining Jobs
Jobs usually execute in parallel, but you can set them to execute in sequence. In this case, we’re running a single job.
jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest Note: ubuntu-latest defines the run environment.
Defining Steps
The first step involves checking out the repo, which is crucial for a Hugo site as themes are added as submodules.
steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v2 with: submodules: true Building Hugo
Using lowply’s container for Hugo:
- name: Build Hugo uses: lowply/build-hugo@v0.88.1 Deploying to GitHub Pages # After building the Hugo site on every master push, the next step was deploying the output to a separate repository for GitHub Pages.
- name: deploy changes to a repo uses: tagus/git-deploy@v0.3.2 with: changes: public repository: git@github.com:john-nicholson/john-nicholson.github.io.git ssh_key: ${{ secrets.REPO_DEPLOY_KEY }} name: John email: john@thenicholsons.online clean_repo: false Note: Create a repository secret in the repository options where the action is triggered.
The Final Output # After the action runs, you can observe the standard output stats from Hugo:
| EN ------------------+----- Pages | 48 Paginator pages | 0 Non-page files | 0 Static files | 20 Processed images | 0 Aliases | 2 Sitemaps | 1 Cleaned | 0 Check out your other repository, and you’ll see the output of your newly automated Hugo site!

I am a technology leader who has spent most of my career working where technology, organisations and change meet.
That has taken me through software engineering, cloud, architecture, DevOps, platform engineering, large-scale transformation and, increasingly, AI. Much of my work has been in complex or regulated environments where the interesting challenge is rarely choosing the technology. It is working out how to change the surrounding system without losing control of what matters.
That is also what I tend to write about here.
I am interested in flow: how work moves, where it gets stuck, what creates unnecessary friction and how organisations can make meaningful change more often. I am equally interested in architecture, but less as a collection of diagrams and more as a way of shaping capability, constraints and future choices.
More recently, a lot of my thinking has moved towards AI and agency. Not just models or individual use cases, but the wider questions: what context an AI system needs, how organisations encode knowledge and policy, how decisions should be made, what should remain deterministic, and where human judgement is genuinely necessary.
Those topics connect more than they first appear to.
A value stream, a cloud platform, an approval process, a knowledge graph and an agentic system are all, in different ways, attempts to shape how information and decisions move through a system. That is probably the common thread behind most of the writing on this site.
A few other things that shape the perspective # I have worked across consultancy, software businesses, education and public-sector-adjacent environments, and I have spent time on both sides of the supplier/client boundary. I am also involved in charity governance and church leadership. Those contexts are very different, but they repeatedly raise the same questions about trust, accountability, stewardship, risk and how much control is actually useful.
I also write occasionally about personal systems, learning and ADHD. Attention is a constraint too, and some of the same ideas that apply to organisational flow turn out to apply surprisingly well to individual work.
This is not intended to be a polished personal-brand site or a substitute for a CV. It is a place to develop and publish ideas, including some that are still changing.
The older posts are intentionally still here. They are part of the record of how my thinking has developed, even where I would write them differently now.
If you are looking for the conventional career summary, LinkedIn is the better place for that. This site is more about the ideas behind the work.
Any opinions expressed here are my own and do not represent any organisation I work for, have worked for, or advise.

Choosing the Right Environment for Hugo Development: My Journey to Containers # When it comes to setting up a development environment for Hugo, there are numerous options available. My journey in selecting the most suitable one was guided by a desire for efficiency and minimal impact on my primary workstation. Here, I share my experience and rationale behind choosing containers over other methods.
Why Not Traditional Installations? # Installing development tools directly on my laptop is a route I tend to avoid. From my experience, such installations inevitably lead to a point where a complete system purge becomes necessary. This approach, although straightforward, doesn’t align well with my preference for maintaining a clean and efficient workspace.
Considering the Alternatives # Virtual Machines (VMs) # Using a VM is a viable option, offering the convenience of wiping it clean post-use. However, my past experiences with VMs—particularly performance issues and the overhead of maintaining another system image—make this less appealing to me.
Cloud-Based Virtual Machines # Cloud VMs are definitely an attractive option, especially considering the scalability and resources they offer. However, their dependency on a stable internet connection poses a limitation. Any connectivity issue directly impacts productivity, which is a significant drawback for development work.
Why I Chose Containers # After careful consideration, I decided that using a container for Hugo development was the optimal choice for me. Containers offer several advantages:
Efficient Resource Usage: Containers share the kernel with the host, avoiding the overhead associated with full virtualization. Space-Efficiency: They are generally more space-efficient compared to VMs. Portability: Containers can be easily transported and replicated across different machines. Ease of Use: Starting a container is straightforward, especially when using pre-built images. Implementing Hugo with Containers # For my Hugo environment, I chose the klakegg/hugo image, which met all my requirements without the need to create a custom image. This choice streamlined my development process significantly.
To work with Hugo in this containerized environment, the process is remarkably simple. On any machine with Docker installed, I can quickly set up my Hugo environment. Here’s the command I use:
docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):/src -p 1313:1313 klakegg/hugo:0.74.1 server -D This command allows me to test my Hugo site locally, including draft posts, with minimal setup and without impacting my primary system’s configuration.
Conclusion # Choosing the right environment for development is key to a smooth and efficient workflow. In my case, containers emerged as the ideal solution, balancing ease of use, resource efficiency, and isolation from my primary operating system. This approach has significantly streamlined my development process with Hugo.

My journey in selecting the most suitable one was guided by a desire for efficiency and minimal impact on my primary workstation. Here, I share my experience and rationale behind choosing containers over other methods.

Jekyll # Jekyll This ruby based generator has gained alot of traction. It is used extensively for githubpages even powering the main githubpages site.

It is probably just the ammount of time I’ve spent working in ASP.net but there were a couple of points where it feels a little inconsistent.
Hugo # Hugo This Go based tool is pretty powerful. I was recommend it by @sympodius, which immediately says alot to me. Go is an interesting laguage so I’m intrigued to see how this works.
Templating # Immediately, hgo puts me at eas with the way botht he templates and and the architypes provide consistent formatting. Initially I wasn’t sure what I through of including the template as a submodule, that sid I quite like the idea and it certainly helps to speed up the build time.
Perfomance # As expected for anything written in go it is FAST. I really do mean fast where with other systems the dependencies take some time to intially load with Hugo it was immediate. Another small point to not is it was docker capable straight away, with the jekyll setup I had to provide a bunch of different options to the server to get automatic reloads to work, with Go this is the default configuration.
Clarity # Overall I’ve found the hugo system fairly simple to get up and running. I especially appreciated the quick create templating with architypes. The folder structure makes a great deal of sense and well this site has been generated using hugo.
Summary # I’ve tried 2 so far and I have to say I do likeboth of these generators though I’ve chosen for the moment to stick with Hugo. The next step will be a custom theme, and I’m sure I’ll write about it as I go along.

I’ve had the privilege to get early access to The Unicorn Project by Gene Kim. Set within Parts Unlimited a large manufacturing and retail organisation that is struggling to come to terms with software as a first class citizen. Yes for those of you who have read The Phoenix Project this story is set in the same organisation and you see many of the same characters and events that occurred. In fact this tale follows another character within the narrative that was only briefly introduced before, namely a developer.
In all honesty I have been extremely excited about this book since I heard rumour of it being in the works. The Phoenix Project changed the way so many organisations approached I.T. and it still does. Within my company (IJYI) it is unofficially mandatory reading (or listening) for all employees. However where the phoenix project focused on IT operations, the unicorn project promised to focus on software and product development, a promise it has not failed to deliver on.
The starting picture is familiar to many developers, slow bureaucratic processes surrounding any changes that may occur. Outright fear of deploying any changes so completed work ended up being hoarded until the business was practically screaming for the features. Within the book Gene introduces the rebel alliance a group of people willing to put their necks on the line to help the business and others even though it is against policy. This, above all, within the book rang so true for me. Before I started IJYI I was involved in the development of a large scale insurance product. With thousands of lines of code, it was to be critical to a new line of business for the organisation and yet after a year and a half it had yet to be used. It was around this time that myself and Chris (co-founder of IJYI) both separately joined this team. In this team we found a number of kindred spirits. Testers, developers, the business representatives who were all willing to put their jobs on the line and try something new, which was completely against the organisations policy, Agile. The program manager for the initiative much like a character in Gene Kim’s book ran interference on the reporting requirements and we had 3 months to get this huge unworkable system out. Long story short,it worked. There were ups, downs and lots in between but it stand clear in my mind as an example where bottom up leadership provided clear value. I’m happy to say I truly felt like part of the rebel alliance.
As you can see I completely related to the story woven in the Unicorn Project, and yet as with all work based fables like this I still find I am learning things, whether it is new approaches to innovation or a new means of communicating the power and joy of declarative programming. The unicorn project is easy to read and will provide you with inspiration within your daily work.
The unicorn project is available for pre-order now and will be release on November 19 2019.

I’ve been reading The Goal as well as The Phoenix Project. Whilst there are many important principals in these novels and I highly recommend them. I wanted to highlight one in particular. The danger of too much Inventory or unfinished work. Recently I was working on an Agile project. This team conformed to the scrum framework zealously, the application architecture was solid, the team were beyond excellent, we had fantastic and driven product owner. Yet despite all of this we consistently missed our sprint goal. Each retrospective we looked at the process adjusted and tried again. We reduced sprint lengths reduced the number of stories in a sprint, inflated our estimates for the stories, and quite a number of other adjustments, nothing seemed to resolve the issue. We were confounded nothing seemed to resolve what was happening. Finally Matt the Scrum Master suggest one last thing.
The entire team would only work on one story at a time
Essentially we set a Work in Progress limit of 1 not for a given column i.e. Test but for the entire stream. As you can imagine there was a lot of resistance to this. In a team primarily made up of contract resource this seemed crazy, can you imagine the burn rate? As with the old concept of a factory with contract resource in IT you always aim to get your pound of flesh, this is expensive resource you want to keep them busy. At least that is the common practice.
Despite the resistance the team committed to the restriction. Throughout the sprint only 1 story was allowed to be in progress at any one time. Amazingly the first story was signed off by the product owner within a day or two. I was astounded, the team were encouraged and it only got better from there. True through put was achieved within the sprint, not by carrying stories over.
What caused this? what hadn’t we seen before?
I think for myself despite all the rhetoric and the adherence to ceremony, my measure of productivity was fundamentally askew. Busy != Productive even if it is with prep or other items in the sprint if it does not help get the highest priority items from left to right then It’s probably not something that should be done.
For the team it forced the brain hive to work as one, with only one item to work on the team was forced to swarm on every problem, this helped to transfer knowledge as significantly improved resolution speed.
